pages.title: Organization settings
pages.description: Name your organization, restrict e-mail domains, check SSO and members.
pages.md:
Open the command palette (`⌘K` / `Ctrl+K`) and run **Organization settings…**.

## What you can set

- **Organization name** — shown in the admin panel.
- **Allowed e-mail domains** — the domains your members sign in with
  (`acme.com`, `acme.co.uk`). Used as the default domain for SSO sign-in.
- **SSO status** — whether an SSO worker is configured and whether you are
  currently signed in through it.
- **Members** — listed once SSO is connected. Without SSO the panel shows a
  "Connect SSO" prompt.
- **Audit log** — available on the Team plan (or always, when self-hosted
  without billing).

## Offline and self-hosted

Without a backend, the name and domains are stored only in this browser
(local-only mode). Nothing is sent to a server.

pages.title: Signing in
pages.description: What each sign-in status means and how to fix the common errors.
pages.md:
Signing in is optional — Lumen works fully offline without an account.
An account unlocks persistent collab rooms, cloud sync and Smart search.

## Status messages

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Signed in** | A session is active. | Nothing. |
| **Signed out** | Cloud sign-in is available but you are not signed in. | Open **Sign in** in the toolbar. |
| **Sign-in not configured** | This build has no auth provider (local-only mode). | Self-hosters: see [Enable accounts](#enable-accounts). Everyone else: keep working locally. |
| **Sign-in error** | The provider could not be reached or rejected the request. | See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting). |

## Enable accounts

Set these in `.env.local` and rebuild:

- **Email / OAuth (Supabase)** — `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` and
  `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, then `npm install @supabase/supabase-js`.
- **Enterprise SSO (WorkOS)** — `VITE_WORKOS_ENDPOINT`; see
  [Single sign-on](/account/sso/).

## Troubleshooting

- **Network error / provider unreachable** — check your connection, VPN or
  corporate proxy, then retry. Lumen keeps working locally meanwhile.
- **Invalid email or password** — reset the password from the provider's
  e-mail, or use the OAuth buttons.
- **Session expired** — sign in again; your local documents are untouched.

pages.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
pages.description: Sign in with your company's identity provider through WorkOS.
pages.md:
Lumen supports SAML and OIDC single sign-on through
[WorkOS](https://workos.com). Your organization's admin connects the
identity provider once; members then sign in with their work e-mail domain.

## Signing in

1. Open **Sign in** in the toolbar.
2. Enter your organization's e-mail domain (for example `acme.com`).
3. Complete the sign-in at your identity provider. You are returned to
   Lumen and signed in.

## Error reasons

When SSO fails, Lumen returns with `?sso=error&reason=…`:

| Reason | Fix |
|---|---|
| `no_sso_connection` | No organization is set up for that domain. Ask your admin to add the domain in WorkOS. |
| `state_mismatch` | The sign-in was started in a different browser or took longer than 10 minutes. Start again. |
| `access_denied` | Your identity provider refused the sign-in — ask your IT admin to assign you to the Lumen app. |
| `code_exchange_failed` | The SSO worker could not verify the sign-in. Usually a wrong `WORKOS_API_KEY` / `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID`. |

## Self-hosting

Deploy `edge-workers/auth/` (see `DEPLOY.md` §5b) and set
`VITE_WORKOS_ENDPOINT` to the worker URL.

pages.title: Auto-tag + link suggestions
pages.description: AI assistants that read your workspace and propose structure.
pages.md:
Lumen ships two opt-in agents that scan a note (and the rest of your
workspace) and suggest improvements. Both run from `⌘K`.

## Auto-tag this note

Command: `🏷️ Auto-tag this note`.

The agent reads the active document, looks at the existing `tags:`
vocabulary across every note in your workspace, and proposes 3–7 tags
that fit. You see the proposals first — accept, edit the list, or skip.
Accepted tags merge into the note's frontmatter idempotently (existing
tags are preserved).

**Why workspace-aware**: a fresh note about machine learning shouldn't
get a brand-new `ml` tag if you already use `machine-learning`
elsewhere. The agent prefers existing tokens and only invents new ones
when nothing fits.

## Suggest wiki-links

Command: `🔗 Suggest wiki-links`.

For each phrase in the active note that overlaps with the title or
intro of another note, the agent proposes wrapping the phrase in a
`[[Title|phrase]]` wiki-link. You review the list (each suggestion comes
with a one-line "why") and accept all / none.

Only literal substrings that already appear in your note become links —
the agent never invents prose. Phrases already inside a wiki-link or
markdown link are skipped automatically.

## Ask Workspace

Inside `⌘K → Search workspace…` → **Ask Workspace** tab. Hybrid retrieval
over your notes plus a chat model on top of the matched context. Multi-turn — the
conversation persists for the open dialog.

## Privacy

All three agents go through the same `chat()` pipeline and respect the
**Local AI** toggle (`⌘K → Switch to local AI (WebGPU)`) and the
[AI policy](/ai/privacy/). When local AI is on, prompts stay on your device — `web-llm` runs the model via WebGPU and
the workspace never leaves your browser.

pages.title: AI cost — usage meter and answer cache
pages.description: See what your AI requests cost, and avoid paying twice for the same answer.
pages.md:
Lumen calls the AI provider you choose with your own API key. Two
features keep that bill visible and small. Both run locally on your
device.

## Usage meter

Command: `AI: Usage & Cost This Month` (`⌘K`).

For the current month it lists requests, input and output tokens, and an
estimated cost per provider and model.

- **Exact counts** come from the provider whenever its API reports them:
  OpenAI, Claude (including prompt-cache reads and writes), Gemini and
  Mistral, both for regular and streamed answers.
- **Estimated counts** (about 4 characters per token) are used when the
  provider reports nothing, and are marked as estimated.
- **Local models** (Ollama, in-browser WebGPU) are counted at $0.
- **Prices** come from a built-in table of list prices, dated in the
  report. Treat them as an estimate; your provider's dashboard is the
  real bill. Models missing from the table are counted but not priced.

Usage stays in this browser's storage. It isn't synced and is never sent
anywhere.

## Answer cache

Command: `AI: Answer Cache…`.

Some commands transform a given text deterministically: auto-tag,
translate, diagram from text, action items, chart from data and heading
suggestions. When you run one of them again on exactly the same input
with the same provider and model, Lumen reuses the stored answer
instead of paying for a new one. Cache hits appear in the usage report.

- Change the text, the model or the provider and the request goes to the
  model again.
- Answers expire after 30 days. At most 500 are kept, and the oldest are
  dropped first.
- From the command you can turn the cache off (every request then asks
  the model) or clear it.
- Cached answers are stored in this browser's IndexedDB, on this device
  only.

## Claude prompt caching

With Claude, long system prompts and long documents sent as context
(about 8,000 characters or more) are marked for Anthropic's prompt cache.
A follow-up request on the same document within about five minutes reads
that prefix at roughly 10% of the normal input price. The usage report
shows these cache reads separately.

## Cost mode

Command: `AI: Cost Mode (Economy / Balanced / Quality)…`.

| Mode | Small tasks¹ | Other requests | Context per question² |
|---|---|---|---|
| Economy | Small model | Small model | ~2,000 tokens |
| Balanced (default) | Small model | Your chosen model | ~5,000 tokens |
| Quality | Your chosen model | Your chosen model | ~12,000 tokens |

¹ Tags, heading suggestions, completions and commit messages. The small
models are GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Mistral
Small. Local providers (Ollama, WebGPU) are never rerouted, and a
request that names its own model is left alone.

² **Ask Workspace** reads the matching notes in full, then sends only
the parts relevant to your question. Each note is split at its
headings, the sections are ranked against the question (BM25), and the
best ones are kept within the budget. Every note also sends its heading
outline, so the model still sees how it is structured. Notes that
already fit are sent unchanged.

## Batch over a folder (half price)

Command: `AI: Batch over a Folder (half price)…`, then `AI: Check Batch Jobs`.

To tag, summarise or translate many notes, Lumen sends them as one job to
the provider's batch API: OpenAI's Batch API or Anthropic's Message
Batches. Both charge half the normal price and return results within
24 hours.

1. Pick what to do (tags, a one-line `summary` in the front matter, or
   a translation into a new `name.<language>.md` file next to each note)
   and which folder to process.
2. Lumen shows the number of notes and an estimated cost before
   anything is sent. Each note counts as one AI prompt against your
   plan's quota.
3. Later, run `AI: Check Batch Jobs`. When a job has finished, Lumen
   shows how many notes will change and how many files will be created,
   and applies the changes only after you confirm. Notes that are open
   in a tab are skipped, and existing files are never overwritten by a
   translation.

Batch jobs need the OpenAI or Anthropic provider. Their usage appears
in the usage report at batch prices.

pages.title: AI doctor
pages.description: One check of the whole local-AI stack, from Ollama to the on-device engines, with the exact fix for each row.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → AI: Doctor (diagnose local AI)`. Each row shows what the doctor found, and
every row that is not OK also gives the fix: a command to copy, a button
that applies the fix, or a link. The checks only read state. None of them
downloads a model or sends your notes anywhere.

## What it checks

| Row | OK when | Fix when it is not |
|---|---|---|
| AI policy and preferred executor | always (context) | — |
| Ollama server reachable | `/api/version` answers | install / `ollama serve`; `OLLAMA_ORIGINS` on a 403; rebuild with the address allowed when the CSP blocks it |
| Chat, configured, tool-calling and embedding models | installed | `ollama pull …` (button: *Download now*) |
| WebGPU, WebAssembly | available | use Ollama, or a browser with WebGPU |
| Vault storage | room left, durable | *Keep my data* |
| Service worker | registered | — |
| **CSP for the local services** | the page may connect to ports 8010 and 8787 | rebuild with `VITE_CSP_CONNECT_EXTRA` |
| Grammar (LanguageTool), research | they answer | `docker compose -f docker/local-ai.yml up -d`; *Use the local services* points both at that compose file |
| **Converted-model host** (Opus-MT, Nakdimon) | a host is set and the registry lists its files | waits for the owner's host choice (plan 15.9), then the conversion workflow |
| **Local translation** | Chrome's translator or Opus-MT can take English↔Hebrew | M2M100 downloads on first use with consent, or use Chrome |
| **English spelling** | the shipped dictionary flags a known misspelling | reload |
| **Hebrew spelling dictionary** | Hspell is installed | *Download (5.7 MB)* |
| **Niqqud** | Nakdimon is hosted | same as the converted-model host |
| **Image descriptions** | always available (download with consent on first use) | — |
| An executor the agents can use | one is available | `ollama serve` or the AI settings |

*Run one golden case per agent* runs a real model call for each agent
that has a golden case. Agents without one are listed as *skipped*, so you
can see which ones are missing.

## Local services

`docker/local-ai.yml` starts LanguageTool on port 8010 and the research
service on port 8787. The production CSP already allows both
(`http://localhost:8010`, `http://localhost:8787`), and the doctor checks
that the build you are running still allows them.

pages.title: Image descriptions on this device
pages.description: Alt text for pasted and attached images — OCR, a local vision model, or a captioning model in the browser. Nothing is sent to the cloud.
pages.md:
An image with no alt text, or with only its file name (`IMG_1234`,
`Screenshot 2026-…`), gets a real description. Lumen tries, in order:

1. **OCR** — an image that is mostly text (a screenshot, a slide, a scan)
   gets that text: the first line as alt text, the full text as the image
   title, so search finds it.
2. **A vision model in Ollama** on this machine (qwen2.5vl, gemma3, llava,
   moondream…), asked for one sentence in the note's language.
3. **A captioning model in the browser** — Florence-2 base-ft (Microsoft,
   MIT, ≈ 224 MB), with SmolVLM-256M-Instruct (Hugging Face, Apache-2.0,
   ≈ 189 MB) when Florence-2 cannot load on this device or gives nothing
   usable. Both run in a background worker (WebGPU when available) and
   describe in English; the description is then translated into the note's
   language with [local translation](/ai/translation/). When no local
   translation can take the pair, the English description is kept.
4. Otherwise the file name stays. Lumen never invents alt text.

Every description is checked before it is written: not empty, at least two
words, not the file name or a camera placeholder, not the prompt read back.

## Downloads

The browser models are downloaded from Hugging Face only after you agree
in a dialog that shows the model, its size, its licence and its
attribution. That dialog appears only when you run
`⌘K → Images: alt text from OCR / local vision`. Pasting an image never
asks; it uses a browser model only after you agreed to it once from the
command. Declining stops there: Lumen does not offer the fallback model
in the same run.

To turn off automatic alt text for pasted images, set
`lumen.ai.imageText` to `off`.

## Measured

| Check | Status |
|---|---|
| Order, consent, fallback, validator, translation | unit tests (`caption.test.ts`, `captionWorker.test.ts`) |
| Quality: ≥ 80% of the 50 images of the caption golden set rated ≥ 4 / 5 | **not measured yet** — the set's Crossmodal-3600 part is built by the golden-sets workflow and the other 20 images and all ratings are the owner's (plan 15.11, 15.15) |
| Speed and memory on real hardware | not measured: the models are not reachable from the build machine |

pages.title: Local agents
pages.description: Every AI command runs through one local agent runtime — the model proposes, tools execute, validators decide, and an improvement agent steps in when there is no answer.
pages.md:
Lumen's AI commands are **agents**: a definition of what to ask the
model, which tools it may call, what shape the answer must have and how
to check it. One runtime (`src/agents/runtime.ts`) runs every definition
against the first available **executor**, on this device whenever it
can:

| Executor | Where it runs | Tool calling | JSON output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ollama | a local Ollama server | native (`tools`) | native (`format`) |
| web-llm | your browser, on the GPU | JSON-ReAct protocol | JSON mode |
| `chat()` | whatever provider you selected | JSON-ReAct protocol | prompt |

The **AI policy** (`⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy"`) decides whether a
cloud provider may ever be contacted. The default on a fresh install is
*local only*.

## What a run does

1. Picks the first available executor in the agent's preference order.
2. Sends the system and user prompts. When the agent has tools and the
   executor cannot call them natively, the prompt teaches the JSON-ReAct
   protocol: the model answers `{"tool": …, "args": …}` or
   `{"final": …}`, one JSON object per turn.
3. Executes each tool call. Tools that write or reach the network need a
   permission the command grants explicitly; a model can never write
   where you did not expect.
4. Parses the final answer (JSON when the agent declares a schema) and
   runs the agent's **validators** — a Mermaid diagram must compile, an
   ECharts option needs series and axes, tags must exist, offsets must
   fall inside the text.
5. When there is no usable answer, the **improvement agent** (the
   critic) diagnoses the failure and proposes one change for a retry —
   temperature 0 with the validator's error fed back, then a larger
   model tier — up to two retries. If that still fails, the run ends
   with **suggestions** you can act on: start Ollama, allow the app's
   origin (`OLLAMA_ORIGINS`), pull a model, split the document, try
   another executor, or allow the cloud.
6. When the retries are used up, a small local model (the tiny tier)
   reads the failure and may add one or two suggestions in plain
   language. The suggestions panel opens on its own; pressing a
   suggestion does it (pulls the model, switches the executor, changes
   the policy) and runs the command again.

Every run is recorded on this device: `⌘K → "AI: Recent Agent Runs"`
shows the executor, model, tool calls, retries and failures of the last
50 runs.

## AI settings

`⌘K → "AI: Settings (local agents)"` gathers everything in one panel:

- the AI policy;
- **who runs the agents** — automatic (Ollama → browser → chat provider)
  or one executor first, with a live *available / not available* check
  for each;
- the Ollama address and model, with the models already installed;
- the in-browser model, the device card (WebGPU, f16, a VRAM budget
  estimate) and the catalogue, with models too large for this device
  disabled;
- the grammar (LanguageTool) and research (SearXNG worker) addresses;
- your writing-style profile on/off;
- the last ten agent runs.

The panel writes the same settings the runtime reads; nothing is stored
twice. The VRAM budget is a heuristic from the browser's coarse hints,
not a measurement.

## Transcription and embeddings on this device

Speech recognition and text embeddings do not go through a chat model:
they run in a second worker on
[transformers.js](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js) with
ONNX Runtime (WebGPU when the GPU is usable, wasm otherwise). The ONNX
Runtime files are served from this app's own origin (`/ort/`), so no CDN
is contacted; the models come from Hugging Face and are cached in the
browser.

| Task | Model | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Voice memo (`🎙 Voice memo`) | `onnx-community/whisper-small` | ≈ 250 MB | WebGPU; multilingual (Hebrew included) |
| Voice memo on a strong GPU | `onnx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo` | ≈ 800 MB | WebGPU, ≥ 6 GB budget |
| Voice memo without WebGPU | `onnx-community/whisper-tiny` | ≈ 40 MB | wasm, slower |
| Smart search embeddings | `Xenova/multilingual-e5-small` | ≈ 120 MB | 384 dimensions, ~100 languages |

Under *local only* the cloud Whisper API is never used; under *local
first* it is the fallback when the local path fails; under *cloud* it is
used directly.

## Ollama from the hosted app

A page served from `https://lumen-md.vercel.app` may only call your
local Ollama when Ollama allows that origin:

```
OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://lumen-md.vercel.app ollama serve
```

(on macOS: `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_ORIGINS https://lumen-md.vercel.app`
and restart Ollama). Without it Ollama answers `403` and the improvement
agent suggests exactly this fix. The desktop app and `localhost`
development builds need no change.

## Research, grammar and search on this machine

`docker/local-ai.yml` starts three services:

| Service | Port | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| SearXNG | 8888 | Metasearch, no API key |
| research service | 8787 | The same worker Lumen deploys (`edge-workers/research`), run with `wrangler dev`: page extraction plus SearXNG search |
| LanguageTool | 8010 | Grammar and spelling checks |

```
docker compose -f docker/local-ai.yml up -d
```

Then `⌘K → Research: Settings → SearXNG on this machine` and enter
`http://localhost:8787`. Research questions are planned and answered by
your local model; quotes are still verified word for word against the
pages. Under *local only* a research service off this machine or network
is refused. On a fresh install with the *local only* policy, SearXNG is
the default research provider.

## Evaluating a local model

`npm run eval:agents` runs twelve fixed cases — most of them in Hebrew —
through the real agent runtime against your Ollama, and writes a report
to `eval/results/`:

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model llama3.1:8b --only tagger-he,tasker-he
```

In CI the same cases run against a **fake Ollama server**
(`npm run fake-ollama`, `scripts/fake-ollama.mjs`) over real HTTP: the
runtime, the Ollama executor, the parsers and validators are exercised on
every pull request without a GPU. Only model quality needs the live run.

Every check is deterministic (Hebrew share of the letters, required and
forbidden words, list lengths, length limits, a pattern), so two models
or two prompt versions can be compared on the same numbers. The report
lists each case with pass/fail, attempts (retries the improvement agent
asked for) and time. The reference answers in
`src/agents/eval/fixtures.ts` run in CI through each agent's own parser
and validators, so a broken fixture is caught before a long GPU run.

pages.title: Local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU)
pages.description: Run AI prompts entirely on your device — private, offline-capable, no per-token cost.
pages.md:
Lumen routes every AI command through `chat()`. With `useLocalAi`
toggled on (and a WebGPU-capable browser), prompts go to a model
running in your tab via [web-llm](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm) —
nothing leaves the machine.

## Switch on

```
⌘K → "Switch to local AI (WebGPU)"
```

The first prompt downloads a model **sized for this device** — the
model manager probes the GPU (WebGPU, `shader-f16`, device memory) and
picks the largest model of the task's tier that fits, from about 0.4 GB
(SmolLM2 360M) to 6 GB (Qwen3 8B, Gemma 2 9B). Pick one yourself with
`⌘K → "AI: Local Models (WebGPU)"`, which also shows what is already
downloaded and lets you download a model ahead of time. Weights are
cached in the browser; later prompts start instantly.

Inference runs in a **Web Worker**, so the editor stays responsive
while a model loads or generates, and a toast reports download progress
at 5 % intervals.

## When to use it

- You're on a plane / café / corporate network without API access.
- The note contains secrets you don't want to put into a hosted LLM.
- You want predictable cost — local inference is free after the
  one-time download.

## When not to use it

- Long-context tasks (>4k tokens) — the 8B model loses coherence.
- Latency-sensitive flows — local inference is ≈ 5–10× slower than
  GPT-4o-mini for the first token.
- Older laptops — the model needs ≥ 4 GB of GPU memory.

## How to fall back

What happens when WebGPU (or Ollama) isn't available depends on your
**AI policy** (`⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy"`):

- **Local only** (the default on a fresh install): nothing leaves the
  device. The command stops with a clear message and the agent's
  suggestions (start Ollama, pick a smaller model, use a WebGPU browser).
- **Local first**: a reachable Ollama server answers first (also when a
  cloud provider is selected); in-browser WebGPU takes the request when
  Privacy Mode is on; only then the cloud provider with your key. An
  installation that had only a cloud key before policies existed keeps
  this behaviour until you choose.
- **Cloud**: the selected cloud provider is used directly. An
  installation that had a cloud provider selected before policies
  existed starts here.

Under **Local only** every other path that would send content to a third
party stops as well: smart-search embeddings, Whisper transcription,
batch jobs, fine-tuning, Claude web search, a remote research service and
the public LanguageTool API (a LanguageTool or SearXNG on this machine or
network is fine).

See [Local agents](/ai/local-agents/) for how every AI command runs
through the local agent runtime.

## Pick a different model

`⌘K → "AI: Local Models (WebGPU)"` lists the curated catalog for this GPU
(size, tier, downloaded, recommended). "Automatic" lets the model manager
choose per task: small models for tags and completions, larger ones for
translation and documents, Hermes (function calling) when an agent needs
tools, Qwen2.5 Coder for the product builder.

## Privacy claim

When `useLocalAi` is on AND `localLlmAvailable().available === true`,
prompts never leave your tab. The only network requests web-llm makes
are the initial weight downloads (from `huggingface.co` mirrors) plus
optional telemetry that you can disable. No prompt content is
transmitted.

pages.title: MCP integration (Claude Desktop, Cursor, …)
pages.description: Expose your Lumen workspace as a Model Context Protocol server so any AI agent can read, write, and search your notes.
pages.md:
Lumen ships an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) server out of the
box. Configure it once and Claude Desktop / Cursor / any MCP-aware
client can read your workspace, write new notes, and run substring
searches — from inside the chat, with no extra UI.

## Install

The server isn't published to npm yet, so build it from the repository
(Node 22 or later):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md/mcp-server
npm ci
npm run build          # → mcp-server/dist/index.js
```

## Configure Claude Desktop

Edit `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lumen": {
      "command": "node",
      "args": ["/path/to/lumen-md/mcp-server/dist/index.js"],
      "env": {
        "LUMEN_WORKSPACE": "/Users/you/Documents/Lumen"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Restart Claude Desktop. A 🔌 icon appears in the chat input — your
Lumen workspace is now part of Claude's context.

## Tools the agent gets

| Tool | Args | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `read_note` | `path` | The full markdown body |
| `write_note` | `path`, `content` | Confirmation string |
| `list_notes` | — | Newline-separated list of every `.md` / `.txt` |
| `search_workspace` | `query`, `limit?` | Substring matches with line numbers |
| `append_note` | `path`, `content` | Adds to the end of an existing note |
| `delete_note` | `path`, `confirm: true` | Refuses without `confirm: true` (safety guard) |
| `update_frontmatter` | `path`, `set?`, `unset?` | Patch YAML keys; body untouched |
| `list_tags` | — | Tag → count map across the whole workspace |
| `get_backlinks` | `path` | Notes that contain `[[wiki-link]]` to this one |

## Examples

> *Read my note about deep learning and summarise the open questions.*

Claude calls `search_workspace("deep learning")` → top hits → `read_note`
on each → composes a summary with citations linking back to your notes.

> *Capture my last 5 messages as a new note titled "Meeting prep — Q3".*

Claude calls `write_note("meetings/2026-q3-prep.md", "...")` — your note
is written to `LUMEN_WORKSPACE` at once; the web app sees it after the
next Git pull (see below).

> *Tag every note under `2024/` as archived.*

Claude calls `list_notes` → filters to `2024/` → loops
`update_frontmatter(path, { set: { status: "archived" } })`. Bodies stay
intact; only frontmatter is rewritten.

> *Which notes link to "Project Aurora"?*

Claude calls `get_backlinks("projects/project-aurora.md")` → returns
every note containing `[[Project Aurora]]`.

## Security boundary

The server **refuses any path containing `..` or absolute paths**. An
agent can only see files under `LUMEN_WORKSPACE`. Run the server only
against directories you'd be comfortable showing the agent.

## Sync with the web app

The MCP server is a Node process — it can't reach OPFS in your browser
directly. The standard pattern: bind your Lumen workspace to a Git repo
(`⌘K → Git: clone repository…`), clone the same repo to the path you set
in `LUMEN_WORKSPACE`, and use `git pull` / push to keep both sides in sync.

pages.title: Hebrew niqqud on this device
pages.description: Add or remove vowel points (niqqud) in Hebrew text with a model that runs in your browser.
pages.md:
Three commands in `⌘K`, on the selection — or the whole note when nothing
is selected:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Hebrew: add niqqud** | Points every Hebrew word. Existing points are replaced. |
| **Hebrew: add partial niqqud** | Points only the words the model finds ambiguous, the way modern texts point a word that could be read two ways. |
| **Hebrew: remove niqqud** | Strips the points. Needs no model. |

English, code, numbers and punctuation pass through unchanged. Before
anything is written, Lumen checks that the letters themselves did not
change — only points are added or removed.

## The model

[Nakdimon](https://github.com/elazarg/nakdimon) (Elazar Gershuni, MIT,
≈ 21 MB) runs in a background worker with ONNX Runtime on WebAssembly,
so it works on any device, without a GPU and offline once downloaded.
It is downloaded only after a dialog that shows its size, licence and
attribution, verified against the checksum in `models/registry.json`,
and kept on this device.

The download is served from Lumen's own model host, which is not set up
yet; until then *add niqqud* says the model is not available, and
*remove niqqud* works as usual.

## Measured

On the dev split of the `nikud` golden set, with
`node scripts/golden/evals/nikud.mjs --dev --model Nakdimon.onnx`:

| Part | Sentences | Words fully right | Letters with a wrong mark |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modern (Nakdimon's own held-out test texts) | 10 | 93.6% | 2.8% |
| Classical (Ben-Yehuda: poetry, liturgy) | 15 | 54.9% | 21.3% |
| Letters unchanged (all) | 25 | 100% | — |

Nakdimon is trained on modern Hebrew; classical and poetic text needs the
larger "high quality" model, which is not part of Lumen yet.

pages.title: Privacy and the AI policy
pages.description: What stays on your device, the one setting that decides whether AI may ever use the cloud, and the ledger that records every AI network request.
pages.md:
By default nothing you write leaves this device. Notes are kept in the
browser's private storage, or in a folder on the desktop. They go
somewhere else only when **you** turn on sync, collaboration, or a cloud
AI provider.

## The AI policy

`⌘K → AI: Local or Cloud Policy` decides where an AI request may go:

| Policy | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Local only** | nothing leaves this device: Ollama, the in-browser WebGPU model and transformers.js only. A cloud provider is **never** contacted, not even as a fallback when no local model can answer. |
| **Local first** | local models first; a cloud provider (with your own key) only when none of them can answer |
| **Cloud** | the cloud provider you selected is used directly |

A **fresh install starts on *Local only***. An installation that was set
up for the cloud before policies existed keeps its behaviour (*Cloud*
when a cloud provider was selected, *Local first* when only a key was
configured), so an upgrade never silently changes where your prompts go.

## The privacy ledger

`⌘K → Privacy ledger…` lists every network request the AI features made:
the time, the host, how many bytes went out and came back, why
(cloud AI, a model download, research…), the policy at that moment, and
whether it was **allowed or blocked**. A request the policy forbids is
blocked before it leaves the machine and still appears in the ledger, so
you can see that it was stopped.

The ledger stores **no** prompt, response or header, only the facts above.
It covers AI traffic: provider calls, embeddings, transcription, grammar,
research and model downloads, including the OCR language models fetched
from a worker. Fonts, sync and the app's own files are not AI traffic and
aren't listed.

## Everything else

| Data | Where it lives | Leaves the device? |
|---|---|---|

pages.description: Ask a question and get a note with a quoted source for every claim; check the citations in any note.
pages.md:
## Research: Ask a Question

Command: `🔎 Research: Ask a Question…`.

Lumen searches the web, reads the sources and writes a new note. The
note starts with a short summary, followed by sections, and every claim
carries a footnote. Each footnote holds the passage from the source
that supports the claim:

```md
Roses are pruned in early spring.[^1]

[^1]: [Rose guide](https://example.org/roses) — “Prune roses in early spring, when buds swell.”
```

Choose how Lumen searches with `🔎 Research: Settings…`:

| Search | Needs | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude web search** (default) | AI provider set to Claude (Anthropic) | One request: Claude searches (up to 5 searches), reads and answers. The quotes are copied word for word from the pages by Anthropic. Anthropic bills the searches separately from tokens. |
| **Brave Search** / **Tavily** | Your own API key, and the research service on this deployment | Lumen plans 2–4 searches and reads up to 6 pages. It sends the model only the parts relevant to your question, then **checks every quote against the page it came from**. A quote that can't be found is marked ⚠️ in the note. |

Pages the research read but didn't cite are listed under "Also read".
Every model call appears in `AI: Usage & Cost This Month`. A research
run counts as one prompt against your plan's AI quota.

## Research: Verify Citations in This Note

Command: `🔎 Research: Verify Citations in This Note`.

This works on any note, not only research output. Lumen reads the
footnotes that link to web pages and checks each one:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✅ quote found | The quoted passage is on the page. Quote marks, dashes, case and spacing don't need to match exactly. |
| 🟡 found approximately | At least 85% of the quote's words appear close together on the page. |
| ❌ quote not found | The page is reachable, but the passage isn't on it. |
| 💀 dead link | The page returned an HTTP error. |
| ⚠️ couldn't read | The address was blocked, the page isn't HTML or text, or the request timed out. |
| 🔗 reachable | The footnote has no quote, so only the link was checked. |

Footnotes can be written as `[^1]: [Title](url) — “quote”`, as
`[^1]: url "quote"`, or as just a link.

## The research service

Reading pages and Brave / Tavily searches go through a small worker that
your deployment runs (`edge-workers/research`, set with
`VITE_RESEARCH_ENDPOINT`). Browsers can't fetch other sites directly.

- It only reads public http(s) pages, never internal addresses.
- It reads at most 2 MB per page.
- It forwards no cookies.
- Your search key is passed through for each request and is never
  stored.
- It only answers your app's own origins.

Claude web search doesn't need the service.

pages.title: English spelling on this device
pages.description: Spell-check English notes with a dictionary that ships with Lumen — no LanguageTool account, no request leaves the device.
pages.md:
Lumen's grammar check (`⌘K → Check grammar (LanguageTool)`, and the background
underlines when *Grammar check* is on) has three backends. Which one runs
depends on the AI policy and on what you configured:

| | Under *local only* | Under *local first* / *cloud* |
|---|---|---|
| LanguageTool on this machine or network (`lumen.grammar.endpoint`, e.g. `docker/local-ai.yml` on port 8010) | used | used |
| The public LanguageTool API (`api.languagetool.org`) | **never contacted** | used |
| English dictionary on this device (this page) | used | — |
| Local proofreader model | added when you run the check yourself | — |

Hebrew paragraphs are always checked on this device (rules plus the
optional Hspell dictionary) and never sent anywhere.

## What it checks

- **Words**, against the en-US Hunspell dictionary
  ([dictionary-en](https://github.com/wooorm/dictionaries/tree/main/dictionaries/en)
  4.0, SCOWL word list, MIT AND BSD) through
  [nspell](https://github.com/wooorm/nspell) (MIT), in a background worker.
  The dictionary (≈ 0.55 MB) is part of the app: nothing is downloaded.
- **Only English paragraphs.** Each paragraph's language is detected on
  this device; a French or German paragraph is not marked as misspelled
  English. A paragraph too short to tell follows the rest of the note.
- **Only prose.** Code blocks, inline code, front matter, URLs, e-mail
  addresses, link targets, wiki links, footnote labels, `#tags`, HTML tags,
  ALL-CAPS acronyms, camelCase names and words with digits are skipped.

Hover an underline for up to three suggestions.

## Measured

On the committed dev split of the `spell-en` golden set (25 Moby-Dick
sentences with 32 injected typos), checked by
`node scripts/golden/evals/spell-en.mjs --dev` and by the unit tests:

| Metric | Result | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Typos found | 100% | ≥ 90% |
| First suggestion is the right word | 62.5% | — |
| Right word among the first five | 84.4% | — |
| Correct words marked wrong (clean sentences) | 2.6% | ≤ 3% |

Most false marks are names (*Queequeg*, *Stubb*) and British spellings
(*honour*): the dictionary is American English. The held-out test split
is scored by CI with the set's secret seed.

## Limits

- American English only; other Latin-script languages get no spelling
  check under *local only* unless you run LanguageTool yourself.
- Spelling, not grammar: "their is" passes. For grammar, run LanguageTool
  on this machine or use the explicit check, which adds the local
  proofreader model.
- There is no personal word list yet.

pages.title: Local translation
pages.description: Translate a document on this device, in three layers — Chrome's built-in translator, Opus-MT for Hebrew ⇄ English, M2M100 for the rest — with code and links kept exactly.
pages.md:
`⌘K → AI: Translate Document` translates the whole note into the language
you name. Since plan 6.4 the translation runs **on this device** whenever a
local layer can take the language pair; the cloud or local LLM is the last
resort, not the first.

## The three layers

| Layer | What | Languages | Download |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Chrome's built-in translator | Chrome's on-device Translator API | the language packs Chrome offers (Hebrew included) | a language pack, managed by Chrome, after your consent |
| 2 · Opus-MT | `opus-mt-en-he` (Apache-2.0) and `opus-mt-tc-big-he-en` (CC BY 4.0), converted to ONNX by Lumen, running in transformers.js in a worker | English ⇄ Hebrew | once, through the consent dialog below |
| 3 · M2M100 | `M2M100-418M` (MIT), same worker | about 100 languages, any pair | once, through the consent dialog |
| 3b · the AI model | the translator agent (your configured LLM) | any | — |

Which layer runs is decided by **measured quality**: each layer's chrF on the
`mt-he-en` golden set (NTREX-128, both directions) is recorded in
`src/ai/mt/quality.json`. Opus-MT is the baseline; a layer measured below
it for a pair is never chosen automatically. A layer whose quality has not
been measured yet may still run, and the toast says so ("its quality on
this pair is not measured yet").

The document's language is detected locally (plan 6.5), paragraph by
paragraph: a paragraph already in the target language is left as it is.

## Nothing downloads without asking

Before the first use of Opus-MT or M2M100 a dialog shows what the model
is for, its **size** (hundreds of MB), its **licence** and **attribution**,
and asks. A yes downloads the files once; Opus-MT's files are checked
against the checksums in `models/registry.json` and kept in this browser's
private storage (OPFS). A no leaves the document untouched and the
translation falls through to the next layer that is already available, or
to the AI model. Nothing you write is sent anywhere by the local layers.

Until the converted models are hosted (plan 15.9) layer 2 reports
"the converted models have no host yet", and the toast after a translation
lists the reason each local layer did not run.

## What never changes

Fenced and indented code, inline code, math, YAML frontmatter, every link
and image target, wiki links, autolinks, bare URLs, e-mail addresses,
footnote marks and HTML tags are kept exactly as they were. Only the words
move: headings, list items, quotes and table cells keep their markers. If a
model disturbs a protected span, the line is translated again run by run,
and the result is checked before it replaces your text.

## Measuring

```sh
node scripts/golden/evals/mt.mjs --dev --models <folder with the converted models>
```

prints chrF per layer and direction on the dev split of `mt-he-en`;
`--write-quality` records the numbers that decide the automatic choice. A
layer the harness cannot run where it is executed is reported as
"not measured", with the reason, never as a number.

pages.title: Dynamic blocks reference
pages.description: The fenced code-block languages that Lumen renders as live, interactive previews.
pages.md:
Lumen's killer feature is **dynamic blocks**: write a fenced code block in markdown, and the preview renders it as a chart, diagram, table, map, or live sandbox. Every block degrades gracefully — if rendering fails, you still see the source.

## Quick-reference table

| Fence | Renders as | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ` ```mermaid ` | Inline SVG diagram (flowcharts, sequence, gantt, class, state, ER) | Mermaid v11; lazy-loaded |
| ` ```chart ` | ECharts (line / bar / pie / scatter / heatmap / radar / boxplot / treemap / sunburst / sankey) | YAML or JSON spec |
| ` ```csv ` / ` ```tsv ` | Sortable / filterable DataTable + auto-chart suggestion | Title via `title="..."` |
| ` ```json-table ` | DataTable from a JSON array | Array of objects required |
| ` ```sql ` / ` ```pandas ` / ` ```object ` / ` ```data ` | Tabular display via the shared `DataBlock` renderer | `pandas` parses DataFrame `to_dict()` shape |
| ` ```map ` / ` ```geojson ` | Leaflet map (tile, markers, polygons, popups) | GeoJSON or YAML map-spec |
| ` ```dot ` / ` ```graphviz ` | Graphviz diagram via WASM | Rendered locally — no Kroki dependency |
| ` ```plantuml ` / ` ```puml ` | PlantUML via kroki.io | Network egress; opt out via privacy mode |
| ` ```abc ` | ABC music notation (renderable score) | Abcjs |
| ` ```model ` | 3-D model viewer (`<model-viewer>`) | GLB / GLTF |
| ` ```embed ` | Universal embed (YouTube, Vimeo, Twitter, Loom, CodePen, oembed) | URL on the body line |
| ` ```html ` / ` ```html-preview ` | Sanitized HTML preview | DOMPurify allowlist; no JS executes in the page |
| ` ```svg ` / ` ```live-svg ` | Sanitized inline SVG preview | Same hardening as HTML |
| ` ```live-js ` | JS sandbox (Worker isolate) with console output | Stdout/stderr/error states; timeout-protected; `shared` = one REPL scope per document (see below) |
| ` ```live-lua ` / ` ```lua-live ` | Lua 5.4 (wasmoon WASM) in a Web Worker, with `print`/`io.write` output and return values | Loads on Run; self-hosted wasm (no CDN); `timeout=` ms (default 5000) |
| ` ```live-r ` / ` ```r-live ` | R (webR, WebAssembly): printed output, messages, warnings, errors and base-graphics plots | Loads on first Run (~45 MB, self-hosted, cached); `timeout=` ms (default 30000); base R + bundled recommended packages, no CRAN installs |
| ` ```live-ruby ` / ` ```ruby-live ` | Ruby 3.4 (ruby.wasm) in a sandboxed Web Worker: `puts`/`warn` output, the last value (`=> …`), errors with `block:<line>` | Loads on first Run (~30 MB, self-hosted, cached); `timeout=` ms (default 10000; a runaway loop is killed); full stdlib (`require "json"`, `set`, …), no gems; fresh VM per run; no network, storage or JS bridge |
| ` ```playground [react\|vue] ` / ` ```web-playground ` | A small multi-file web project run live: files separated by `--- name.ext ---` lines (HTML, CSS, JS, JSX, TS, JSON); Preview, a tab per file, and a Console | Runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin (no access to your documents); JSX / TypeScript via Sucrase; `react` / `react-dom` (18) and `vue` (3, with the template compiler) are provided offline — other packages aren't; entry is `main.*`; `height=` px |
| ` ```live-css ` | Sandboxed iframe HTML+CSS preview | `srcdoc` + sandbox flags |
| ` ```live-glsl ` / ` ```glsl ` / ` ```shader ` | GLSL fragment shader on a quad | Hot-reloads on edit |
| ` ```bibtex ` / ` ```bib ` | Citation list (formatted from BibTeX) | Click → copy citation |
| ` ```database ` | Workspace-wide database query (markdown frontmatter as the "table") | Lumen-native query DSL |
| ` ```insights ` / ` ```jsonl ` | JSONL analyzer: conclusions, freq, charts, file generators | No external model |
| ` ```code-doctor ` / ` ```fix-json ` | Malformed JSON/JSONL repair with diff + accept-fix UI | 7-pass tolerant tokenizer |

## Live JavaScript — shared scope (REPL across blocks)

By default every ` ```live-js ` block runs in its own fresh Web Worker, so nothing one block defines is visible to another. Add `shared` to the fence to turn the blocks of a document into one REPL session:

````markdown
```live-js shared
const prices = [12, 7, 30]
function total(xs) { return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }
```

Some prose in between…

```live-js shared
console.log(total(prices))   // 49
```
````

- All `shared` blocks of the open document use **one worker**, and its global scope persists across runs and across blocks. Top-level `const` / `let` / `var`, `function` and `class` declarations become globals of that worker, so later runs and later blocks can use them. Declarations nested in blocks, functions or loop heads stay local.
- As in a browser console, running a block again may redeclare its names, and top-level `const` bindings can be reassigned by later runs.
- Blocks share state in the order they **run**. Each block runs when it renders and when you click **Run**; runs are queued and execute one at a time.
- `shared=name` (for example ` ```live-js shared=physics `) gives a separate named scope inside the same document. Different documents never share a scope.
- **Reset scope** (shown on shared blocks) discards the worker and every global in it; the next run starts fresh. Re-run the blocks you depend on afterwards.
- Sandboxing is unchanged: the worker has no DOM and no access to the page, shared mode adds no module or network-import support (the page CSP still applies inside the worker), and a run that exceeds the 8-second timeout is stopped. A timeout terminates the worker, which also resets the scope.
- An unused scope is disposed five minutes after the last shared block of that document unmounts.

## Live Lua

````markdown
```live-lua height=200 timeout=3000
local function fib(n) return n < 2 and n or fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end
for i = 1, 10 do io.write(fib(i), " ") end
print()
return _VERSION
```
````

Click **Run** to execute. Nothing is downloaded until then; the ~270 KB `glue.wasm` is bundled with Lumen and served from the same origin, so it works offline and under the app's CSP. Each run gets a fresh Web Worker and a fresh Lua state:

- `print` and `io.write` stream to the output panel; values `return`ed from the chunk are shown after a `→`.
- Errors show the line (`block:2: boom`).
- A runaway loop is stopped after `timeout` ms (100–60000, default 5000) by an instruction-count hook, and the page kills the worker if it stops responding. **Stop** cancels a run.
- The Lua heap is capped at 64 MB and captured output at 200 000 characters.
- The standard libraries are available except process and file access: `os.exit`, `os.execute`, `os.getenv`, `os.remove`, `os.rename`, `io.open`, `io.popen`, `io.read`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile` and `package` are removed. Lua cannot reach JavaScript objects.

## Security & hardening

All HTML, SVG, and embed renderers funnel through `src/lib/markupSanitizer.ts`. The sanitizer:

- Strips every `on*` attribute via a prefix-matching hook (not just the named list, so future handlers like `onpointerdown` are caught).
- Blocks `style` attributes containing `expression(...)`, `url(javascript:...)`, or `behavior:`.
- Allows only image-MIME `data:` URIs (everything else, including `data:text/html`, is dropped).
- Rejects `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, and unknown protocols.

Each dynamic block is wrapped in an `ErrorBoundary` so a single broken block doesn't take down the whole preview.

## Lazy loading

Every block is `React.lazy`-imported. A block's library (Mermaid, ECharts, Leaflet, …) loads only when a note that uses it is opened, so adding block types never grows the startup bundle. That bundle has a size budget, checked on every pull request (`scripts/bundle-budget.mjs`).

## Authoring a new block

See [Plugin SDK](/plugins/sdk/) — every block is a React component registered with `registerPlugin`. The `pluginSystem` wires its fence language to a tag, mounts via `Suspense`, and routes it through the renderer pipeline.

## Web Playground

````markdown
```playground react height=260
--- App.jsx ---

export default function App() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return <button onClick={() => setN(n + 1)}>Clicked {n} times</button>;
}
--- main.jsx ---


createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render();
--- style.css ---
button { font: 16px system-ui; }
```
````

- **Files:** `--- name.ext ---` starts a file. A body without markers is one file (`main.jsx` for React, `main.js` otherwise). `index.html` is the page body (default `<div id="root">`, or `<div id="app">` for Vue); its `<script>` tags don't run, so put code in files.
- **Imports:** relative imports between files (with or without the extension), CSS / JSON files, and the provided `react`, `react-dom`, `react-dom/client`, `react/jsx-runtime` and `vue`.
- **Isolation:** each Run loads a fresh runner document in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin and its own Content-Security-Policy. The project can't read the app's storage, cookies or page.

sections.heading: Live JavaScript — shared scope (REPL across blocks)
sections.text: By default every markdown Some prose in between… live-js shared=physics `) gives a separate named scope inside the same document. Different documents never share a scope. Reset scope (shown on shared blocks) discards the worker and every global in it; the next run starts fresh. Re-run the blocks you depend on afterwards. Sandboxing is unchanged: the worker has no DOM and no access to the page, shared mode adds no module or network-import support (the page CSP still applies inside the worker), and a run that exceeds the 8-second timeout is stopped. sections.heading: Live Lua
sections.text: live-lua height=200 timeout=3000 local function fib(n) return n < 2 and n or fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end for i = 1, 10 do io.write(fib(i), " ") end print() return VERSION ` Click Run to execute. sections.heading: Security & hardening
sections.text: All HTML, SVG, and embed renderers funnel through src/lib/markupSanitizer.ts. sections.text: See Plugin SDK — every block is a React component registered with registerPlugin. The pluginSystem wires its fence language to a tag, mounts via Suspense, and routes it through the renderer pipeline.

pages.title: End-to-end encryption for collab
pages.description: Add a room password and no relay, signaling server or sync server can read your document.
pages.md:
Lumen's WebRTC mesh is unencrypted by default: peers sync the Yjs
document directly, so a signaling server that relays messages, a
`y-websocket` persistence server, or anyone who joins with the room
link can read the content. Setting a **room password** switches the
room to an end-to-end encrypted transport. Document content is then
only ever readable by peers that know the password.

## Turn it on

```js
// Either:
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "open-sesame-12345");

// Or append to the share link:
//   #room=lumen-bright-river-77&password=open-sesame-12345
```

Every peer in the room must use the same password. A peer with the
wrong password can still connect, but it only receives ciphertext it
can't decrypt. Nothing is applied to its document, and it sees a
"Can't decrypt this room" error.

> Putting the password in the URL hash keeps it out of HTTP requests
> (browsers never send the `#fragment`), but it still lands in browser
> history and anywhere you paste the link. For anything sensitive,
> share the room link and the password through different channels.

## How it works

Each peer keeps **two** Yjs documents:

| Document | Contents | Attached to the network? |
|---|---|---|
| Plaintext doc | Text, comments, everything the editor shows | **No.** It stays in the tab. |
| Transport doc | One append-only `Y.Array` of ciphertext envelopes | Yes (y-webrtc, and y-websocket if configured) |

1. **Key derivation:** PBKDF2-SHA-256, 200 000 iterations, salt
   `lumen.collab.v2|<room name>`. The same password in two different
   rooms gives two unrelated keys.
2. **Outbound:** each local edit to the plaintext doc produces a Yjs
   update. Edits made in the same tick are merged into one update,
   encrypted with AES-GCM-256 under a fresh random 12-byte IV, and
   appended to the transport array as `{ v: 2, iv, ct }`. The format
   version and the snapshot flag are bound into the GCM tag as
   additional authenticated data.
3. **Inbound:** each envelope that appears in the transport array (from
   a peer or from the persistence server) is decrypted and applied to
   the plaintext doc with origin `e2e-remote`. The outbound listener
   ignores that origin, so received edits are never encrypted again
   (no update loop). If decryption fails, the envelope is dropped and
   the user sees an error. Unauthenticated bytes are never applied.
4. **Late joiners:** a peer that joins later receives the whole
   transport array through the normal Yjs sync, decrypts every envelope
   and rebuilds the document. Yjs buffers updates that arrive before
   their dependencies, so envelopes can be decrypted in any order.
5. **Compaction:** when the array grows past 500 envelopes, the peer
   that just wrote one encrypts a full-state snapshot (`s: 1`) and
   deletes only the envelopes it has already applied. A peer that has
   ever failed to decrypt something never compacts, so it can't throw
   away history it couldn't read.

## Who can read what

| Party | Document text & comments | Room name | Envelope count, sizes, timing | Presence: names, colours, cursor anchors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Peer with the password | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Peer without the password | **No** | Yes | Only through a persistence server it can reach | **No** — it can't complete the WebRTC handshake |
| Signaling server | **No** | Yes | Traffic shape only (its messages are encrypted with the password) | **No** |
| `y-websocket` persistence server | **No** (it stores only ciphertext) | Yes | Yes | **No** — Lumen publishes no presence to it |
| Network eavesdropper | No (WebRTC is DTLS-encrypted anyway) | Depends on the signaling transport | Traffic shape | No |

### Persistent rooms store only ciphertext

With [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) the `y-websocket` server
syncs the **transport** doc. Its database holds the envelope array and
never a key, so a leaked server backup reveals no document content. A
peer that joins later still needs the password to read the history.

## Limits: what this does *not* protect

- **Awareness / presence reaches every peer that holds the password.**
  The room password is also given to y-webrtc, which encrypts all
  signaling and BroadcastChannel traffic with a key derived from it, and
  peer connections are DTLS-encrypted — so the signaling server and peers
  *without* the password never see display names, colours or cursors.
  Presence itself is not wrapped in Lumen's envelopes, though: every
  password holder sees it. Cursor positions are Yjs *relative positions*
  (item IDs: client id + clock, no document text). The persistent
  `y-websocket` server receives no presence from Lumen.
- **Metadata:** room name, number of peers, number and size of
  envelopes, and when they are written. Size and timing can hint at
  how much is being typed.
- **Integrity of the history as a whole.** Each envelope is
  authenticated, but a malicious relay or persistence server can
  *drop* or *withhold* envelopes, or delete them from the array. That
  makes peers diverge or lose edits, but it can never inject or alter
  content. Replayed envelopes are harmless because Yjs updates are
  idempotent.
- **Anyone with the password.** All peers who know it are trusted
  equally. A peer with the password can also delete envelopes from the
  shared array.
- **Weak passwords.** The key comes only from the password and the room
  name, both of which a server operator knows. An attacker holding the
  ciphertext can run an offline guessing attack, slowed by 200 000
  PBKDF2 iterations per guess. Use a long passphrase.
- **No forward secrecy, no key rotation inside a room.** A password
  that leaks later decrypts all stored history. To rotate, create a
  new room with a new password (see below).
- **Local storage.** Version-history snapshots and saved files on each
  peer are plaintext on that device. Use a Vault password
  (`⌘K → Encrypt document`) for at-rest encryption.

## Rotating

The key is tied to the room, so the clean way to rotate is to move to
a new room with a new password:

```js
localStorage.setItem("lumen.collab.password", "new-stronger-passphrase");
```

Then leave and start a fresh room, seeding it from your current
document. If you change the password while staying in the same room,
peers on the old password get "Can't decrypt" errors, and the old
history stays encrypted under the old key on any persistence server.

## Trade-offs

- A misplaced password locks everyone out. Treat it like any shared
  secret and share it through a side channel (Signal, 1Password, etc.).
- The PBKDF2 derivation runs once per password and room. That is about
  100 ms on modern devices, but noticeable on old phones.
- Each edit batch adds about 40 bytes of overhead (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing). Long sessions grow the array until compaction
  kicks in at 500 envelopes.

pages.title: Persistent rooms
pages.description: Keep a collaboration room alive when every peer has left, with a small y-websocket server you run yourself.
pages.md:
A plain [WebRTC room](/collab/webrtc/) lives only in the browsers that are
in it: when the last person leaves, the room is gone (whoever saved the
note keeps their copy). A **persistent server** keeps each room's
document, so anyone can join later and find the latest version, even when
nobody else is online.

## Run the server

`sync-server/persistent-server.js` is a small
[y-websocket](https://github.com/yjs/y-websocket) server that stores every
room on disk with LevelDB.

```bash
cd sync-server
npm install @y/websocket-server y-leveldb
PORT=4444 node persistent-server.js        # ws://localhost:4444
```

- **Storage:** `YJS_STORAGE_DIR` (default `./.yjs-persistence`). On Fly.io,
  Render or Railway, point it at a mounted volume. The Docker compose
  bundle uses `/data/yjs`.
- **Access token:** start it with `COLLAB_TOKEN=<a long random string>`
  and it accepts only clients that send the same token. Without one,
  anyone who knows a room name can read the room's (encrypted) updates
  and add their own.
- **Health:** `GET /healthz` answers `200 {"ok":true}`.
- Put it behind TLS (`wss://`) before you expose it.

`DEPLOY.md` has the Fly.io steps.

## Point Lumen at it

Set it when you build Lumen:

```bash
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_URL=wss://collab.example.com
VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN=<the same COLLAB_TOKEN>   # if the server has one
```

Lumen then connects to the server alongside the peer-to-peer mesh. Where
billing is configured, persistent rooms need a Pro or Team plan; a
self-hosted build without billing has them on.

## What the server can read

Nothing, in a room with a password. The server stores only the
AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes, never the text. Rooms created today
have 128-bit random names and are end-to-end encrypted, so the token is
a second gate, not the only one. What the server does see: room names,
and the size and timing of updates. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/#persistent-rooms-store-only-ciphertext).

pages.title: Real-time WebRTC collaboration
pages.description: Multi-cursor editing over a peer-to-peer mesh — no server account, no central log of your doc.
pages.md:
Lumen ships a real-time collab mode powered by [Yjs](https://yjs.dev)
over WebRTC. Open a doc, share the room link, and every keystroke
syncs to every peer in <30 ms.

## Start a session

`⌘K → Start collaboration`. A toast confirms the room name + copies
the share link to your clipboard:

```
https://lumen.app/#room=lumen-bright-river-77
```

Anyone with the link enters the same Y.Doc. Their cursor + selection
appears in your editor, coloured by their auto-assigned chip.

## Awareness UI

Each peer publishes:

- **Display name** — random adjective+noun combo, e.g. "Marble".
- **Colour** — auto-picked HSL hue.
- **Cursor + selection** — re-published on every selection change.

The editor renders peer cursors with a small floating name tag above
the caret. A peer's selection highlights with a translucent version of
their colour. The list of active peers shows in the status bar.

## End-to-end encryption

Without a password, the room is **not** end-to-end encrypted. Peers sync
the plaintext Yjs document, so any signaling server that relays
messages, any `y-websocket` server and anyone with the room link can
read it.

Set `localStorage["lumen.collab.password"]` (or append `&password=…` to
the share link) to change that. The editor's document then stays
local, and only AES-GCM-256 ciphertext envelopes (key = PBKDF2 of the
password, salted with the room name) go to the mesh and to any
persistence server. Peers without the password receive only ciphertext
and see a "Can't decrypt this room" error.

The password also encrypts y-webrtc's signaling, so a peer without it
can't connect at all and relays never see presence (names, colours,
cursor positions) — only peers holding the password do. Metadata such
as the room name and the volume and timing of edits is still visible.
A wrong password therefore looks like an empty room: Lumen asks before
sharing your document into it rather than forking the room silently. See
[End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/) for the full threat model.

## Rooms evaporate when the last peer leaves

WebRTC is peer-to-peer — there's no server holding the doc. The doc
state lives in each peer's Y.Doc, replicated over the mesh. Once
everyone leaves, the state is only in the OPFS workspace of whoever
saved it. To get persistent rooms (the Notion / Google Docs feel),
enable [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/).

## Comments / annotations

Inline comments anchor to text ranges via Yjs `RelativePosition`, so a
comment on "neural networks" stays attached to those words even when
collaborators insert paragraphs above. Open the comments panel from
`⌘K → View comments panel`.

## Performance budget

- Room cap: 20 simultaneous peers (raise via the WebRTC provider's
  `maxConns`).
- Per-update overhead in password rooms: ≈ 40 bytes (IV + GCM tag +
  envelope framing) per edit batch; edits made in the same tick share
  one envelope.
- Initial join: full Y.Doc snapshot synced via the signaling channel
  (≈ 1 KB per 1k characters of doc).

For documents larger than ~50k characters or sessions with >20 peers,
move to [persistent collab](/collab/persistent/) which uses
`y-websocket` + a server-side store.

pages.title: Hebrew and right-to-left
pages.description: Writing in Hebrew (and Arabic) in Lumen — direction per line, the interface in Hebrew, search that ignores niqqud and prefixes, spelling on this device, and exports that keep the direction.
pages.md:
Lumen is built for notes that mix Hebrew and English.

## The interface

`⌘K → Language: …` switches the interface. Hebrew and Arabic flip the
whole layout (sidebar, menus and dialogs mirror). The interface is in 8
languages: English, Hebrew, Arabic, Russian, French, German, Japanese and
Chinese.

## Direction in a note

- **Per line, automatically.** In the source editor each line takes its
  direction from its first strong letter: a Hebrew paragraph aligns right,
  an English one left, and the cursor and selection follow. Code blocks
  and the front matter are always left-to-right.
- **For a whole note:** put `dir: rtl` (or `ltr`) in its front matter.
- **For the editor:** `⌘K → Text Direction: RTL (Right to Left)` (and back
  with *Text Direction: LTR*).

## Search

Workspace search folds niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix
letters ו ה ב כ ל מ ש, so *בבית*, *והבית* and *הַבַּיִת* all find *בית*.
The exact form ranks first. See
[Workspace search](/workspace/search/). Links between notes and heading
anchors compare names the same way, so `[[שלום]]` finds *שָׁלוֹם.md*.

## Spelling, on this device

Hebrew paragraphs are checked **locally**: a final letter inside a word, a
repeated word, a space before punctuation. For spelling against a
dictionary, download Hspell's word list once with

pages.title: Editor modes
pages.description: Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG — pick the one that fits the task.
pages.md:
Lumen has four editor surfaces. Switch with `⌘1` / `⌘2` / `⌘3` / `⌘4`.

## Source (`⌘1`)

Plain CodeMirror 6 with markdown highlighting. Use it when you want to
write fast, see exactly what the file contains, or paste pre-formatted
markdown. The "Smart Insert" pill (`⌘⇧V`) is most powerful here.

**Best for**: writers who think in markdown; data-heavy notes where you
want the fence delimiters visible.

## Split (`⌘2`, default)

Editor on one side, live preview on the other. The split orientation
follows your viewport — horizontal on wide screens, vertical on phones.
Override via the **Scroll orientation** menu in the top bar.

Scroll-link is on by default — both panes track the same heading even at
different content heights.

**Best for**: most authoring sessions. You see the rendered output the
moment you type.

## Preview (`⌘3`)

Read-only render of the markdown. Tables, charts, diagrams, math, embeds
— everything in its final form. Print from here with
`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`, which keeps the colours so PDFs come out
faithful.

**Best for**: reading notes back, proof-reading, sharing your screen.

## WYSIWYG (`⌘4`)

Notion-grade editing on top of Milkdown / ProseMirror. Slash menu (`/`),
inline math, drag-and-drop block reordering. Round-trips to plain
markdown — so a doc you wrote in WYSIWYG opens cleanly in Source.

**Best for**: visual thinkers; rich documents (presentations, decks);
anyone migrating from Notion.

## Toggle without leaving the keyboard

| Key | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘1` | Source |
| `⌘2` | Split |
| `⌘3` | Preview |
| `⌘4` | WYSIWYG |

The mode is remembered across reloads, so you come back to the view you
last used.

## Suggesting mode (track changes)

Turn it on from the command palette ("Turn on suggesting mode (track changes)") or with
the **Editing / Suggesting** pill in the status bar. While it is on, edits
in the Source / Split editor and in WYSIWYG are recorded as
[CriticMarkup](https://github.com/CriticMarkup/CriticMarkup-toolkit), so
the file stays plain markdown:

| You do | Stored as |
| --- | --- |
| Type text | `{++inserted++}` |
| Delete text (Backspace, Delete, cut) | `{--deleted--}` |
| Type over a selection | `{~~old~>new~~}` |
| Write a note by hand | `{>>comment<<}` / `{==highlight==}` |

- Typing next to your own insertion extends it, and consecutive deletions
  merge. Deleting text inside your own `{++ ++}` really deletes it.
- Undo / redo, edits from collaborators, and edits inside code blocks or
  inline code are never turned into suggestions.
- The editor shows insertions underlined in green, deletions struck
  through in red and comments highlighted; the preview renders them as
  `<ins>`, `<del>` and `<mark>`.
- Palette commands: accept / reject the suggestion at the cursor, accept
  all, reject all, next / previous suggestion. All of them work in
  WYSIWYG too; accept all / reject all also work from Preview.
- **In WYSIWYG** suggestions show as underlined insertions and struck-out
  deletions (hover for the author). Typing is recorded as an insertion,
  Backspace / Delete leave the text struck out and step over it, and
  typing over a selection becomes a substitution. Structural edits —
  joining two paragraphs with Backspace — aren't recorded as a
  suggestion and are undone; turn suggesting off for those.
- The status-bar pill shows how many suggestions the document contains.
- **Who suggested it.** When you are signed in, each new suggestion is
  followed by an author tag — a comment holding only `@name`, e.g.
  `{++new text++}{>>@Tal<<}`. The tag belongs to its change: accepting
  or rejecting the change removes it too. Hover a suggestion to see
  "Suggested by …"; the preview shows the name as a small comment.
  Typing inside someone else's suggestion keeps their name on it.

## TypeScript checks in code blocks

Run **Enable TypeScript checks in code blocks** from the command palette.
In the Source / Split editor, every ` ```ts `, ` ```typescript ` and
` ```tsx ` block (and JavaScript blocks, see below) is then checked by the
real TypeScript compiler:

- Errors get a wavy underline — hover it for the message (`TS2322: …`).
- Hovering a name shows its type (and its JSDoc, if any).
- Completions pop up while you type (after `.` or a few letters;
  `Ctrl-Space` forces them).
- Each block is checked on its own (its declarations don't leak into
  other blocks), in strict mode against the ES2022 and DOM libraries.
  Imports of npm packages aren't resolved and aren't reported.
- JavaScript blocks (` ```js `, ` ```javascript `, ` ```live-js `) get
  syntax errors, hover and completions; add `// @ts-check` as the first
  line to also get type errors.
- ` ```live-js shared ` blocks are checked together per scope
  (`shared=name`), in document order — a later block sees the names an
  earlier one declared, exactly as when they run. Re-declaring a name
  there is allowed.

The compiler (~1.3 MB compressed) runs in a background worker and is
downloaded only after you turn the setting on; it is not part of the
offline app shell. The setting is remembered.

pages.title: Smart Insert (⌘⇧V)
pages.description: Paste anything into one dialog — Lumen detects the type and wraps it in the right block.
pages.md:
`⌘⇧V` opens a single dialog with one big text area. Paste **anything**
and Lumen figures out what to do with it — across 19 detectors, from
specific (a YouTube URL) to general (a code block whose language is
sniffed from the content).

## The detectors, in order

| Order | Match | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | YouTube / Vimeo / Spotify / Twitter / TikTok / Reddit / GitHub Gist / Figma / Maps / 8 more | ` ```embed ` |
| 2 | Bare HTTPS URL on a single line | Markdown link `[url](url)` |
| 3 | `$$…$$` or `\begin{equation}…\end{equation}` | Math fence |
| 4 | `flowchart LR …`, `sequenceDiagram`, `gantt`, … | ` ```mermaid ` |
| 5 | `digraph G { … }` | ` ```dot ` |
| 6 | `@startuml … @enduml` | ` ```plantuml ` |
| 7 | `X:1 T:Test K:C …` (ABC notation) | ` ```abc ` |
| 8 | `@article{…}` | ` ```bibtex ` |
| 9 | `{ "type": "FeatureCollection", … }` | ` ```map ` (GeoJSON) |
| 10 | YAML with `view:` + `type:` / `source:` | ` ```database ` |
| 11 | YAML with `series:` + `xAxis:` | ` ```chart ` |
| 12 | `CREATE TABLE / INSERT INTO / SELECT …` | ` ```sql ` (parsed to table) |
| 13 | JSON array of homogeneous objects | ` ```json-table ` |
| 14 | Other valid JSON | ` ```json ` |
| 15 | HTML with `<script>` / `<svg>` / `<canvas>` | ` ```htmlpreview ` (interactive iframe) |
| 16 | Other static HTML | Converted to markdown |
| 17 | `name,age\nalice,30\n…` | ` ```csv ` (table + chart suggestions) |
| 18 | Tab-separated rows | ` ```tsv ` |
| 19 | Code that sniffs as JS / TS / Python / Rust / Go / Java / C / C++ / PHP / Ruby / Dockerfile | ` ```<lang> ` |
| 20 | Anything else | Plain markdown — inserted as-is |

The first match wins. The detection badge in the dialog shows you
exactly what was identified ("Detected as: 🔗 YouTube embed") and a
dropdown lets you override.

## The preview pane

The dialog renders the converted markdown in a preview area below the
input. Live-updates as you type. You see exactly what's about to land
in the doc before you commit with ⌘↵.

## Insert position

- **At cursor** — uses the editor's exposed `insertText` handle so the
  surrounding selection is replaced cleanly.
- **Append** — adds to the end of the doc with two newlines.
- **Replace** — swaps the entire doc (use sparingly).

## Examples

> Paste "https://twitter.com/elonmusk/status/1585841080431321088"

→ Detected as: 🐦 X / Twitter embed → wraps as ```` ```embed ````.

> Paste "name,age\\nalice,30\\nbob,25"

→ Detected as: 📊 CSV table → wraps as ```` ```csv ```` and Lumen
suggests a bar chart based on the column types.

> Paste a multi-line `function fetch(url) { … }`

→ Detected as: 💻 JS code → wraps as ```` ```js ```` with Shiki
highlighting.

## Keyboard shortcut

`⌘⇧V` everywhere. Also reachable via:

- The toolbar's **Insert** menu → first item, marked with ✨.
- The command palette (`⌘K`), search "insert anything".

pages.title: Writing tools
pages.description: Theme settings, voice memos and dictation, the canvas, sync conflicts and the app's dialogs.
pages.md:
Each of these has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## Theme settings

**Theme settings…** in the command palette changes the colours, the
accent, the editor's font, size and line height, and the width of the
text, live. The **Contrast** section shows whether the text and the
accent are readable against the background. **Export** saves the theme as a
file and **Import** reads one back.

## Voice memos and dictation

Speak instead of typing. The quick mode writes what you say straight into
the note with the browser's speech recognition. The memo mode records the
audio, turns it into text and a summary, and inserts them as a voice-memo
block. Under the local-only AI policy this runs on your device; nothing is
sent anywhere. A pill at the bottom shows that the microphone is on; its
stop button ends the recording.

## Canvas

A whiteboard beside your notes: sticky notes, text, shapes, arrows,
frames and images on an infinite canvas, with pan, zoom, undo and redo.
Each canvas is saved in the vault as a `.tldr` file and saved again as you
draw.

## Sync conflicts

When the same note changed on this device and in the cloud since the
last sync, Lumen shows both versions side by side. Changes that don't
overlap are merged for you; for each part that does, choose this device's
or the cloud's version. You can also keep one side as a whole, or cancel
and decide later.

## Dialogs

Questions and confirmations open as small dialogs. **Enter** confirms,
**Escape** cancels, and focus goes back to where it was.

pages.title: Send feedback
pages.description: Report a bug, an idea or a question as a GitHub issue or as text to copy. Lumen has no feedback server, and nothing is sent until you click.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → Help: Send feedback`, or with **Report a problem…** at the
bottom of the [AI doctor](/ai/doctor/).

Lumen has no feedback server. The form turns what you write into the text of
a GitHub issue, and you choose what happens to it:

- **Open on GitHub** opens github.com in a new tab with the issue form filled
  in (title, text and a label for the kind). You check it there and submit it.
  You need a GitHub account.
- **Copy text** puts the same text on your clipboard, for an e-mail or
  anywhere else.

Until you click one of those two buttons, nothing leaves your device. The form
makes no network request, and the preview shows exactly the text that will be
sent.

## What goes in

| Part | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Kind, title, description | always | what you wrote |
| App and browser details | ticked (the default) | Lumen version; web, installed app or desktop; platform; language; AI policy; the browser's user agent |
| AI doctor report | only when you tick it | the doctor's checks of the local AI stack. It never contains note text. Keys, tokens, passwords in URLs and e-mail addresses are removed before it goes in. |
| Screenshot | only when you take one | never part of the text (see below) |

If the issue text is too long for a link, GitHub opens with the title only and
the text is on your clipboard: paste it into the issue.

## Screenshots

**Save a screenshot to attach** asks your browser to capture a screen, window or
tab. The browser shows its own prompt, so you choose what is captured. The
picture is saved on your computer as `lumen-feedback-<date>-<time>.png`. It is
not uploaded. Attach it to the GitHub issue yourself. It may show your notes,
so look at it first.

Browsers without screen capture (most phones) say so and skip this step.

## Diagnostics file

**Save diagnostics** (in the feedback form, on an error screen, or **Save a
diagnostics file** in the command palette) saves `lumen-diagnostics-<date>.json`
on your computer, for you to attach to the issue. It holds what a maintainer
needs to understand a problem, and nothing about what you wrote:

- the version, the app shell (web, installed, desktop), the platform and
  the browser;
- your settings, copied one by one from a fixed list: switches, modes and
  sizes. No note names, folders, keys, tokens or e-mail addresses;
- the vault counted, not read: how many notes, other files and folders, and
  their total size;
- storage: whether the vault is in the browser's private storage, and how
  full it is;
- the last warnings and errors, with every path, URL path, quoted text,
  address and key in them replaced by a placeholder.

Before the file is saved, Lumen checks it once more against the text it
holds in memory (your notes, their names, your keys), and refuses to save a
file that would contain any of it.

## Help in the app

**Help** in the command palette (or F1) opens this documentation inside
Lumen. It is packed into the app, so it works offline, and its search
handles Hebrew prefixes as the website's search does. Every panel and
dialog has a **?** button that opens the help at the part about it.

pages.md:
## Export from Bear

1. Select the notes (or **⌘A** in a tag).
2. **File → Export Notes…**, format **Markdown**, with **Export attachments**
   on. Bear writes one `.md` file per note and a folder of images next to
   each.

## Bring it in

Zip the export folder, or keep it as a folder, then
`⌘K → Import notes (zip / folder: Obsidian, Notion, Lumen)…`. The notes and
their images go into a new folder, `Imported/<name>`, with the image links
intact.

## What changes

| In Bear | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `#tags` and `#nested/tags` | the same inline tags; the tags panel lists them |
| `#multi word tags#` | write them as `#multi-word-tags` (Lumen tags have no spaces) |
| `::highlight::` | kept as text; Markdown has no highlight (use **bold**, or `{==highlight==}` in suggesting mode) |
| `[[note links]]` | the same syntax |
| Sync between devices | Bear's iCloud sync does not reach Lumen; use Git or a shared folder |
