pages.description: Get your notebooks out of Evernote and into Lumen as Markdown, with their images and attachments.
pages.md:
Evernote keeps notes in its own format (ENML), so they are converted on the
way in.

## Export from Evernote

1. Select a notebook (or the notes you want).
2. **File → Export notes…** (or **⋯ → Export**).

## Bring it in

:::note[Coming with the import wizard]
The import wizard (plan W1.26) reads `.enex` exports directly: one folder
per notebook, images and files in place, to-dos as tasks, tags and the
creation and edit dates as properties. Until it ships in your version, use
the HTML route below.
:::

**HTML route**: export the notes as **HTML** (one file per note). In Lumen,
open each file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window — the HTML is converted to
Markdown, images included — and save it to your vault.

## What changes

| In Evernote | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Notebooks and stacks | folders |
| Tags | `tags:` in each note's frontmatter |
| Checklists | Markdown tasks `- [ ]` |
| Encrypted text | stays out (Evernote does not export it in the clear) |
| Reminders, sharing | not in the export |

pages.title: Moving from Google Docs
pages.description: Turn Google Docs into Markdown notes in Lumen — one document, or a whole Drive folder.
pages.md:
## One document

1. In Google Docs: **File → Download → Markdown (.md)**. Older documents
   can also be downloaded as **Word (.docx)**.
2. In Lumen: open the file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window. A `.md` file
   opens as it is; a `.docx` is converted to Markdown with its headings,
   lists, tables and images.
3. Save it into your vault.

## A whole folder

Google Takeout (takeout.google.com → **Drive**) exports a folder of
documents as `.docx`. Unzip it, and open the files in Lumen one by one, or
convert them in bulk to Markdown first and import the folder with
`⌘K → Import notes (zip / folder: Obsidian, Notion, Lumen)…`.

## What changes

| In Google Docs | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Headings, lists, tables, links | Markdown headings, lists, tables, links |
| Comments and suggestions | not in the download; Lumen has its own [suggesting mode and comments](/collab/webrtc/) |
| Right-to-left paragraphs | detected per paragraph — see [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/) |
| Sharing | Lumen is local-first; see [real-time collaboration](/collab/webrtc/) |

pages.title: Moving from Notion
pages.description: Export a Notion workspace and bring its pages, links and attachments into Lumen.
pages.md:
## Export from Notion

1. In Notion: **Settings → Export** (a single page: **⋯ → Export**).
2. Choose **Markdown & CSV**, include subpages, and download the .zip.

## Bring it in

`⌘K → Import notes (zip / folder: Obsidian, Notion, Lumen)…`, then pick the
.zip as it came. Lumen recognises a Notion export by the 32-character IDs
Notion adds to every file name, and:

- removes the IDs from file and folder names (`Plans 1a2b….md` → `Plans.md`);
- rewrites the links between pages to the new names, keeping `#headings`;
- numbers two pages that end up with the same name (`Page 2.md`) and keeps
  the links pointing at the right one;
- imports everything into a new folder, `Imported/<name>`, never over an
  existing note.

## What changes

| In Notion | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| Pages and subpages | Markdown files and folders |
| Databases | a `.csv` per database, next to a folder of its rows; open the CSV as a table, or build a [database view](/workspace/database-views/) over the rows |
| Toggles, callouts | Markdown lists and blockquotes |
| Comments, page history, permissions | not in the export |

## Hebrew

Notion keeps Hebrew page titles in file names; Lumen keeps them as they
are. Right-to-left paragraphs are detected per paragraph — see [Hebrew and
right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/).

pages.title: Moving from Obsidian
pages.description: Bring an Obsidian vault into Lumen — notes, attachments, links and Bases — and what changes on the way.
pages.md:
An Obsidian vault is a folder of Markdown files, and so is a Lumen vault:
nothing has to be converted.

## Bring the vault in

1. In Obsidian nothing needs exporting. Zip the vault folder, or keep it as
   a folder.
2. In Lumen: `⌘K → Import notes (zip / folder: Obsidian, Notion, Lumen)…`
   and pick the .zip or the folder.
3. Lumen recognises the vault by its `.obsidian/` folder and imports every
   note and attachment into a new folder, `Imported/<vault name>`. Nothing
   that is already in Lumen is overwritten. Obsidian's own settings
   (`.obsidian/`, `.trash/`) stay behind.

Details and the full list of what is skipped: [Export and
import](/workspace/export-import/).

## What carries over

| In Obsidian | In Lumen |
|---|---|
| `[[wikilinks]]`, `[[note#heading]]`, `![[embeds]]` | the same syntax |
| Frontmatter properties, `tags:` | the same YAML; the tags panel and database views read it |
| Attachments (images, PDFs) | the same files, the same relative links |
| Callouts `> [!note]` | shown as a quote; Lumen's callouts are `:::note` blocks |
| Canvas (`.canvas`) | kept as files |
| Plugins and themes | not carried over: Lumen has its own [plugins](/plugins/sdk/) |

## Daily habits

- **Command palette**: `⌘K`, as `⌘P` in Obsidian. [Keyboard
  shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/) lists the rest.
- **Hebrew**: the editor and preview are right-to-left aware per paragraph;
  see [Hebrew and right-to-left](/editor/hebrew/).
- **Sync**: Obsidian Sync does not reach Lumen. Use Git, or keep the vault
  in a folder both apps open on the desktop.

## Going back

Your notes stay plain Markdown. `⌘K → Export the whole vault…` gives you a
.zip or a folder that Obsidian opens as a vault.

pages.title: Install Lumen
pages.description: Lumen in the browser, as an installed web app, on the desktop (macOS, Windows, Linux) and on iOS / Android — and what each one stores where.
pages.md:
Lumen is the same app on every platform. The only differences are where
your notes are kept and how the app is updated.

| Platform | How | Notes are kept in |
|---|---|---|
| Browser | open the hosted app, or `npm run dev` from a clone | the browser's private file system (OPFS) |
| Installed web app (PWA) | the browser's **Install** button on the hosted app | the same OPFS; works offline |
| macOS / Windows / Linux | build with `npm run tauri:build` (Tauri 2) | a real folder on disk |
| iOS | `npm run ios:open` (Capacitor, opens Xcode) | the app's storage |
| Android | `npm run android:open` (Capacitor, opens Android Studio) | the app's storage |

## In the browser

Nothing to install. Notes stay in this browser's private storage and never
leave the device unless you turn on sync. **Clearing the site's data
deletes them**, so export the vault (*Export the whole vault…*, see
[Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)) before you clear
browser data, or keep the vault in a real folder.

The minimum versions (set by Tailwind CSS 4) are Safari and iOS 16.4+,
Chrome / Edge 111+ and Firefox 128+.

## Installed web app (offline)

Use the browser's install button (Chrome, Edge) or *Share → Add to Home
Screen* (Safari). The installed app opens without a network: the editor,
highlighting, fonts and your files are all cached.

## Desktop

There are no signed release builds yet, so build from a clone:

```bash
npm ci
npm run tauri:build
```

The desktop app keeps the vault as a folder of plain `.md` files that
other tools (git, Obsidian, a text editor) can open, and keeps secrets in
the OS keychain on macOS and Windows (see
[How Lumen stores your secrets](/security/vault/)). On Linux it needs
WebKitGTK 2.40+.

## iOS and Android

The mobile projects are generated with Capacitor:

```bash
npm ci
npm run ios:open        # or: npm run android:open
```

Then build and run from Xcode or Android Studio.

## Running from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

pages.title: Quickstart
pages.description: Get to your first beautiful Lumen document in 60 seconds.
pages.md:
## 1. Open Lumen

Either visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) (the hosted PWA), install the
desktop app (see [Install Lumen](/getting-started/install/)), or run
locally:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## 2. Type your first note

Hit `⌘N` for a fresh document. Try the smart paste — `⌘⇧V` opens an
"Insert anything…" dialog. Drop in:

- a YouTube link → it wraps as `\`\`\`embed`
- a CSV row → it wraps as `\`\`\`csv` and shows a sortable table + chart
  suggestions
- a SQL `CREATE TABLE` → ditto, parsed as data
- Mermaid `flowchart LR …` → renders as SVG
- A LaTeX equation → math typeset by KaTeX

## 3. Save it

`⌘S` saves to your local OPFS workspace. Open the workspace pane
(`⌘K → Toggle workspace`) to browse / rename / move files. Everything is
just markdown — your notes remain portable.

## 4. Power-user keys

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `⌘K` | Command palette (everything is here) |
| `⇧⌘F` | Focus mode |
| `⌘⇧V` | Smart Insert (auto-detect) |
| `⌘1`–`⌘4` | Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG |
| `⌘H` | Find and replace |
| `⌘O` / `⌘N` | Open / New |

Workspace search is `⌘K → Search workspace…`; the full list is on
[Keyboard shortcuts](/getting-started/shortcuts/).

Now start writing — and explore the [Editor modes](/editor/modes/) for the
heavier surfaces.

pages.description: Every shortcut Lumen binds, where it works, and how to find the rest in the command palette.
pages.md:
On Windows and Linux, `⌘` is **Ctrl**, `⌥` is **Alt** and `⇧` is
**Shift**; the app shows the right keys for your system.
`⌘/` opens this list inside the app.

Everything Lumen can do is a command in the **command palette** (`⌘K`),
which shows each command's shortcut when it has one.

## Anywhere in the app

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `⌘K` | Command palette |
| `⌘/` | Keyboard shortcuts |
| `⌘N` | New document |
| `⌘O` | Open file |
| `⌘S` | Save |
| `⇧⌘S` | Save as |
| `⌘1` / `⌘2` / `⌘3` / `⌘4` | Source / Split / Preview / WYSIWYG |
| `⌘H` | Find and replace |
| `⇧⌘V` | Smart Insert (paste anything, detected and wrapped) |
| `⇧⌘F` | Focus mode (press again to leave) |
| `Esc` | Close the open dialog |

Workspace search has no global key of its own today: open it with
`⌘K → Search workspace…`. Printing is `⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`; `⌘P`
opens the browser's own print dialog.

## In the editor

| Keys | Action |
|---|---|
| `⌘Z` / `⇧⌘Z` | Undo / redo |
| `⌘F` | Find in this note (source editor) |
| `⇧⌥F` | Format the document |
| `Ctrl+Space` | Ask the AI for a continuation (ghost text) |

## In the tab strip and the rich editor

| Keys | Where | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `⌘W` | a focused tab | Close it |
| `↑` / `↓` | a focused block handle | Move the block up / down |
| `Enter` / `Space` | a focused block handle | Put the cursor at the block's start |

pages.title: Welcome to Lumen
pages.description: Why we built Lumen, and what makes it different from Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear.
pages.md:
## Where Lumen fits

There's no shortage of markdown editors — Obsidian, Notion, Typora, Bear,
Logseq, Roam, HackMD, Joplin, Craft. Lumen sits at a specific intersection:

| | Lumen | Obsidian | Notion | Typora | Bear |
| --- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| Local-first (works offline) | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Web app (no install) | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Auto data → table + chart | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ DB only | ❌ | ❌ |
| RTL / Hebrew first-class | ✅ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ | ⚠️ |
| Mermaid + Graphviz + PlantUML + ABC + 3D | ✅ | ⚠️ plugins | ⚠️ Mermaid only | ⚠️ | ❌ |
| Real-time collab | ✅ WebRTC | ❌ | ✅ Pro | ❌ | ❌ |
| Smart search (embeddings) | ✅ Pro | ⚠️ plugin | ✅ AI | ❌ | ❌ |
| MCP for AI agents | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Local LLM (WebGPU) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Open source (MIT) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ | ❌ |

## What we believe

**1. Plain text wins.** Lumen never invents a proprietary format — every
note is portable markdown. Rendering is opinionated; storage isn't.

**2. Data is content.** A spreadsheet inside a note shouldn't need a
plugin. Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and it just becomes a table with
chart suggestions.

**3. AI assists, never gates.** Bring your own key. Disable AI entirely
and Lumen still ships every other feature.

**4. Privacy is structural, not promised.** Local-first storage, transport-encrypted
(WebRTC DTLS) collab, opt-in telemetry that's off by default.

Continue to the [Quickstart](/getting-started/quickstart/) →

pages.description: A local-first markdown editor with first-class data visualisation, RTL, AI, and collab.
pages.md:
## What makes Lumen different


  
    Your notes live in your browser's OPFS. Sync with Git, Dropbox, or your own
    server. Or don't sync at all — Lumen works fully offline.
  
  
    Drop a CSV, JSON, or SQL block and Lumen suggests the right chart with one
    click. Live data via `src=` URLs that auto-refresh.
  
  
    Mermaid · Graphviz · PlantUML · KaTeX · ABC notation · model-viewer ·
    Leaflet maps · ECharts. All first-class.
  
  
    Hebrew and Arabic flow right-to-left throughout the UI. Code blocks, math,
    and the editor stay LTR.
  
  
    Smart search, auto-tagging, link suggestions. Bring your OpenAI key, or
    flip to local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU) — your prompts never leave your
    machine.
  
  
    Lumen ships an MCP server so Claude Desktop / Cursor can read, write, and
    search your workspace through `npx @lumen-md/mcp-server`.
  


## Three lines to get going

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md && npm ci && npm run dev
# open http://localhost:5173
```

Or just visit [lumen.app](https://lumen.app) and start typing — there's
nothing to install.

pages.description: Build your own Lumen plugin in 60 seconds with create-lumen-plugin.

Lumen plugins are tiny ESM modules that register custom blocks, commands, and sidebar panels. The host loads them via dynamic `import(url)` so there's no build pipeline to learn — write a function, ship a JS file. :::caution[Being rewritten] Plugins move to an isolated runtime with a permission prompt per capability (plan 11.2); this page is replaced when that lands. `create-lumen-plugin` isn't on npm yet: run it from `packages/create-lumen-plugin` in the repository. ::: ## 30-second start ```bash npx create-lumen-plugin my-cool-plugin cd my-cool-plugin npm install npm run dev ``` Open Lumen → `⌘K` → **Plugin gallery** → **Load unpacked** → pick `dist/my-cool-plugin.js`. ## The API Every plugin exports a default `activate(api)` function. The `api` argument has these methods: ```ts interface LumenPluginAPI { registerBlock(lang: string, component: ComponentType<{ source, meta }>): () => void; registerCommand(cmd: { id, label, hint?, icon?, action }): () => void; toast(message: string, kind?: "info" | "success" | "warning" | "error"): void; getDocContent(): string; setDocContent(content: string): void; onDocChange(cb: (content: string) => void): () => void; } ``` `activate` may return a cleanup function that runs when the user disables or unloads the plugin — use it to call the unregister fns the API returned, plus tear down any timers / DOM you created. ## Permissions model `lumen-plugin.json` declares the permissions your plugin needs: | Permission | Granted by default | What it lets you do | | --- | :---: | --- | | `register-block` | ✅ | Add a code-fence renderer | | `register-command` | ✅ | Add palette entries | | `register-panel` | ✅ | Add a right-sidebar panel | | `read-doc` | ✅ | Read the active document | | `write-doc` | ✅ | Mutate the active document | | `workspace-read` | ❌ — prompts user | List + read every note | | `workspace-write` | ❌ — prompts user | Create / overwrite notes | | `network-fetch` | ❌ — prompts user | Make outbound HTTP requests | ## Publishing 1. `npm run build` produces `dist/.js` — single ESM bundle, React left external (Lumen ships its own). 2. {c} 📊
{c}
); } ``` That's the whole plugin. ` ```emoji-csv ` blocks now render with the emoji headers everywhere Lumen renders markdown.

pages.title: Plugin signing keys
pages.description: Decide which publishers' plugins Lumen trusts.
pages.md:
Registry plugins can be signed with an **Ed25519** key. Before installing,
Lumen verifies the signature against the keys you trust, so a compromised
CDN cannot ship modified code.

## Manage trusted keys

Command palette → **Trusted plugin signing keys…**

- **Built-in** keys come from the deployment (`VITE_PLUGIN_TRUSTED_KEYS`)
  and cannot be removed from the UI.
- **Your keys** are stored in this browser. Paste the publisher's public key
  and press **Trust key**.

Each key is identified by its **fingerprint** — the SHA-256 of the public
key, in hex. Compare it with the fingerprint the publisher lists on their
website before trusting it.

## Accepted formats

- Base64 SPKI (44 bytes for Ed25519, starts with `MCow`).
- PEM: `-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY----- … -----END PUBLIC KEY-----`.

Generate a key pair with OpenSSL:

```bash
openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out plugin-signing.pem
openssl pkey -in plugin-signing.pem -pubout
```

## Errors

- **Not an Ed25519 public key** — the pasted text is not a 44-byte SPKI
  Ed25519 key (RSA and ECDSA keys are not accepted).
- **Untrusted signer** — the plugin is correctly signed, but by a key you
  have not trusted. Verify the fingerprint, then add the key.

pages.title: Templates
pages.description: Start a note from a template — the built-in ones, the gallery, and the ones you install — and where an installed template lives.
pages.md:
## Start from a template

The command palette lists templates as commands. Pick one and it opens
as a **new, unsaved tab**: it never writes into the note you have open,
and a name that is already taken gets a number (*Meeting notes 2.md*).

## The template gallery

`⌘K → Browse template gallery` opens the gallery: filter by category,
search by name, and **Install** a template. Installing writes it to
`templates/<id>.md` in your vault and adds it to the palette under
**Templates: <name>**. It is an ordinary note, so you can edit it like
any other. With the interface in Hebrew, templates that have a Hebrew
version install in Hebrew.

The gallery's list ships with the app (`public/templates/registry.json`),
so browsing it makes no request to any other site.

## Adding a template to the gallery

See `public/templates/CONTRIBUTING.md` in the repository: one Markdown
file plus an entry in `registry.json` (and a Hebrew file under
`public/templates/he/` when there is one).

pages.title: Web Clipper
pages.description: Save a web page as a clean Markdown note — from inside Lumen (works today), or from the browser extension (still a developer preview).
pages.md:
## Clip from inside Lumen

Two commands save a page into your vault as a clean note, with its source
and the date in the front matter:

- `⌘K → Clip a web page…` — paste a URL; Lumen fetches the page and keeps
  the article (`<article>` / `<main>`), without navigation, ads, forms and
  scripts. Fetching an arbitrary site needs the research service
  ([Research](/ai/research/)); without it, only sites the app's security
  policy already allows can be clipped, and Lumen says so.
- `⌘K → Clip from clipboard` — copy something on a page first; the copied
  HTML (or text) becomes the note.

Clips go into the **Library** folder (**ספרייה** with the interface in
Hebrew), get a number when the name is taken, and open in a new tab.

```yaml
---
title: "How CRDTs Work"
source: "https://martin.kleppmann.com/2020/07/06/crdt-hard-parts.html"
clipped: 2026-04-26
---
```

## The browser extension (developer preview)

`extension/` holds a small Chrome extension (Manifest V3): a **Save to
Lumen** toolbar button and a **Save selection to Lumen** right-click
entry. It converts the selection, or the page's article, to Markdown.

:::caution[It does not save into a vault yet]
The extension sends each clip to `<your Lumen URL>/api/clip`, and when
that fails it opens `<your Lumen URL>/#clip=…`. **No Lumen build answers
either one yet**, so a clip from the extension doesn't arrive in your
vault. Use the commands above until it does.
:::

To try it in developer mode:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md/extension
```

1. `chrome://extensions/` → enable **Developer mode**
2. **Load unpacked** → pick `lumen-md/extension/`
3. In the extension's **Options** page, set your Lumen URL (the default
   is `http://localhost:5173`).

## Privacy

The in-app commands fetch only the page you ask for (through the research
service when one is set up). The extension makes
no request except to the Lumen URL you configure: no tracking and no
telemetry. Its manifest is
[`extension/manifest.json`](https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md/blob/main/extension/manifest.json).

pages.title: How Lumen stores your secrets
pages.description: API keys and tokens are encrypted at rest; in the macOS and Windows desktop apps they go to the OS keychain.
pages.md:
Lumen keeps the secrets it needs on your device: AI provider keys, cloud
tokens (Dropbox, Google Drive, GitHub), the collaboration room password
and the research search key. None of them is sent anywhere except to the
service it belongs to.

## In the browser

Each secret is encrypted with **AES-GCM-256** under a key that WebCrypto
generates as **non-extractable** and keeps in IndexedDB. The raw key bytes
never exist in JavaScript, so a copied browser profile or a storage export
does not reveal your secrets.

What this does **not** protect against: code running inside Lumen's own
origin can still ask WebCrypto to decrypt. That risk is handled by the
Content-Security-Policy and the HTML sanitizer, not by the store.

If the browser has no IndexedDB or WebCrypto (very old engines), Lumen
falls back to plain local storage. The app does not show a warning for
this yet.

## In the desktop app

On macOS and Windows the secrets go to the **OS keychain** (Keychain /
Credential Manager). Lumen keeps only their names, so it knows what to
load.

## Not available yet

There is no master password, lock command or recovery phrase in the app
today. The code for a password vault with a 12-word recovery phrase exists
(`src/storage/vault.ts`) but is not connected to any screen. This page will
describe it when it ships.

## Per-document encryption

Encrypting a single note is a separate feature: `⌘K → Encrypt document`
(AES-GCM-256 with a per-document password, stored as a fenced block at
the top of the file). See [End-to-end encryption](/collab/encryption/).

pages.title: Self-hosting with Docker
pages.description: Run Lumen on your own infrastructure with the docker-compose bundle.
pages.md:
> Lumen is a **local-first** editor — by default everything runs inside
> your browser, no servers needed. This guide is for teams who want to
> own the persistence layer (collab, billing, audit log) on their own
> infrastructure.

## What's in the bundle

`docker-compose.yml` brings up five services on a single VM:

| Service | Port | What |
|---|---|---|
| `lumen-web` | 80 | nginx serving the React SPA + strict CSP |
| `lumen-signal` | 4444 | y-webrtc signaling — peers find each other |
| `lumen-collab` | 4445 | Persistent y-websocket (LevelDB on the `collab-data` volume; health: `/healthz`) |
| `lumen-billing` | 4446 | Stripe webhook handler (optional) |
| `postgres` | 5432 | Entitlements + audit log (collab does **not** write here — a Postgres snapshot archive is not implemented) |

A LevelDB volume (`collab-data`) and a Postgres volume (`postgres-data`)
persist outside container lifecycles.

## Prerequisites

- A Linux VM with **2 vCPU + 4 GB RAM** (Hetzner CX22, DigitalOcean
  basic-2, AWS t4g.medium are all fine)
- **Docker 24+** and **Docker Compose v2**
- A domain pointing at the VM (we'll use `lumen.example.com` below)

## 5-minute install

```bash
# 1. Clone Lumen
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md.git
cd lumen-md

# 2. Copy + edit the env template
cp .env.onprem.example .env.onprem
$EDITOR .env.onprem
#   set LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD to a strong value
#   set LUMEN_BASE_URL to your domain
#   leave LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN empty for now (see the note below)
#   leave Stripe / Sentry / WorkOS empty for now

# 3. Build + start
make onprem-up
```

After ~60 s of image build + container start, visit
`http://<vm-ip>` and you should see the Lumen editor.

:::caution[`LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` in this bundle]
The bundle passes `LUMEN_COLLAB_TOKEN` to the collab server, but not to the
app it builds (`docker/Dockerfile.web` has no `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
argument), and the app has no screen for entering one yet. With a token
set, the app's own clients are refused by the collab server. Keep it
empty, or build the web image yourself with `VITE_YJS_WEBSOCKET_TOKEN`
(see [Persistent rooms](/collab/persistent/)). New rooms are end-to-end
encrypted either way.
:::

## DNS setup (recommended)

Point these subdomains at the VM:

```
lumen.example.com    A    <vm-ip>
signal.example.com   A    <vm-ip>   # or proxy via lumen-web
collab.example.com   A    <vm-ip>
```

Then put a TLS terminator (Caddy, Cloudflare Tunnel, or your existing
nginx) in front. The bundled nginx serves HTTP only; the ports are
mapped 1:1 so a reverse proxy can terminate SSL upstream.

Serve Lumen from the root of its own (sub)domain, as above. The
security headers that ship with the app (the bundled nginx config,
`public/_headers` and `vercel.json`) match root paths. If you build with
a sub-path `base` such as `/app/`, prefix those routes yourself,
including the Web Playground's `/playground-runner.html`, `/assets/*`
and `/playground/*` rules. Without them the playground preview is blocked.

On Netlify the Web Playground preview doesn't load: Netlify's `_headers`
format can't lift the app-wide frame and CSP headers for the runner page.
Cloudflare Pages, Vercel and this Docker image are supported.

## Optional: Billing

If you want to gate Pro features (persistent collab, semantic search,
fine-tune AI) behind a paywall, add Stripe credentials and re-up with
the `billing` profile:

```bash
# In .env.onprem
STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_xxx
STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_xxx

# Bring up with the billing service
docker compose --env-file .env.onprem --profile billing up -d
```

The billing worker runs `wrangler local-mode` so the same code that
powers the Cloudflare deployment also runs in your VM.

## Optional: Sentry telemetry

Set `SENTRY_DSN=https://…@sentry.io/…` in `.env.onprem` to enable
opt-in error reporting. Users still see a toggle in Settings to turn
it off; you control which DSN.

## Optional: SSO with WorkOS

Set `WORKOS_API_KEY=…` and `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID=…` to enable SAML / OIDC
sign-in. A workspace admin pastes their IdP metadata URL into Settings
→ Organisation; WorkOS handles the protocol dance.

## Daily ops

| What | Command |
|---|---|
| Tail logs | `make onprem-logs` |
| Restart everything | `make onprem-down && make onprem-up` |
| Check Postgres | `docker compose exec postgres psql -U lumen` |
| Hard reset (deletes all data) | `make onprem-reset` |

## Backup

The two Docker volumes are the only state Lumen owns:

```bash
# Postgres dump
docker compose exec postgres pg_dump -U lumen lumen | gzip > lumen-pg-$(date +%F).sql.gz

# LevelDB collab snapshots
docker run --rm -v lumen_collab-data:/data -v "$(pwd)":/backup alpine \
  tar czf /backup/lumen-collab-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /data .
```

User documents themselves never leave the browser — they live in OPFS
(Origin Private File System) per browser, per origin. Encourage users
to back up their local content with `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`
(see [Export and import](/workspace/export-import/)).

## Updating Lumen

```bash
git pull
make onprem-up   # rebuilds images + restarts containers
```

Database migrations run automatically on container start
(`docker/postgres-init.sql` is idempotent).

## Sizing for scale

Single-VM 2 vCPU / 4 GB handles:

- Up to ~50 concurrent collab rooms (LevelDB hot cache)
- ~1k entitlement reads / sec
- Linear cost on audit volume — every mutation writes one row

For larger deployments, split:

- `lumen-web` + `lumen-signal` on one VM (stateless, horizontally
  scalable)
- `lumen-collab` on a dedicated VM with a persistent EBS / Block-Storage
  volume
- Postgres on managed RDS / Cloud SQL

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| 502 from `lumen.example.com` | reverse proxy can't reach `lumen-web:80` |
| Editor loads but collab silently fails | `lumen-signal` not reachable; check WS upgrade rules in proxy |
| Pro features stay locked | `lumen-billing` not in the compose profile, or webhook signature secret wrong |
| `pg_isready` fails | `LUMEN_PG_PASSWORD` mismatch between `.env.onprem` and the volume |

If something else breaks, `make onprem-logs` is your friend — the
five-line per-service prefix makes it easy to spot the offender.

pages.description: Publishing a note as a read-only web page — what exists today, the server it needs, and what is not built yet.
pages.md:
:::caution[Not in the app yet]
The publishing code exists (`src/sync/publish.ts`), but **no screen or
command calls it yet**. This page describes what is there, so a host can
set up the server side ahead of the button.
:::

## What it does

`publishNote()` sends a note to a publish server, which stores the rendered
page and answers with its public URL and slug. `unpublishNote()` makes it
private again. A note can be published as **public** or **unlisted**, and
with a password: the body is then encrypted on this device before it is
sent, so the server only ever holds ciphertext. The slug is kept in the
note's front matter (`published: <slug>`) so that publishing again updates
the same page. Publishing needs a plan with cloud features (Pro / Team).

## The server

Any HTTP endpoint that accepts the same JSON works. The reference is a
Cloudflare Worker in `edge-workers/publish`; the steps to deploy it are in
`DEPLOY.md` (section *Publish edge worker*). The app finds the server
through `VITE_PUBLISH_ENDPOINT` at build time. Without it, a development
build (or one on `localhost`) publishes into a local mock, and any other
build refuses with *“VITE_PUBLISH_ENDPOINT is not set”*.

The browser never holds a service key: requests carry the user's session.

pages.title: Database views
pages.description: Notion-style Table / Kanban / Gallery / Calendar over your YAML frontmatter.
pages.md:
The `database` block turns any folder of markdown notes (with consistent
YAML frontmatter) into a queryable collection — and renders the result
as one of four interactive views.

## Tag your notes

Drop YAML frontmatter on every note you want to include:

```yaml
---
type: book
title: Invisible Cities
author: Italo Calvino
rating: 5
status: reading
cover: https://example.com/cover.jpg
---

(body…)
```

The fields you use are entirely up to you — `type` is the only one Lumen
treats specially (it's the row filter).

## Drop a database block

```database
source: books/         # folder under workspace root
type: book             # filter by frontmatter.type
view: kanban           # table | kanban | gallery | calendar
groupBy: status        # for kanban
sortBy: -rating        # prefix '-' for descending
fields: [title, author, rating, status]
cover: cover           # for gallery cards
```

Lumen scans the workspace, matches every note where `frontmatter.type`
equals `book`, and renders the requested view.

## Views

- **Table** — sortable, classic. Click a row to open the note.
- **Kanban** — columns by `groupBy`, draggable cards (coming soon),
  per-card preview of the top 3 fields.
- **Gallery** — cover image + key fields. Set `cover: <fieldName>` to
  pick which frontmatter URL becomes the card image.
- **Calendar** — agenda of every note with a parseable `dateField`.

## Live updates

Edit a note in another tab and the database view re-runs the query
automatically (a `lumen-workspace-changed` event triggers the refresh).

## Tips

- Mix views — keep one big database block at the top of a hub note and
  switch between Kanban and Gallery with the tab strip.
- Combine with **Smart Insert** — drop a YAML spec on an empty line and
  Lumen wraps it as a `database` fence for you.
- The database is read-only inside the block. To edit a row, click its
  title to open the underlying note.

pages.title: Vault Doctor
pages.description: Find broken links, orphans and near-duplicate notes across the workspace, without AI.
pages.md: Command: `🩺 Vault Doctor: Check Workspace` (`⌘K`). Vault Doctor reads every Markdown note in the open workspace folder and opens a report in a new tab. The report links to every note it mentions, so you can click straight through to fix things. It runs entirely on your device and makes no AI calls. | Check | What it finds | |---|---| | Broken wiki links | `[[Note]]` where there is no such note and no such heading in the same note. When exactly one note name is close (same words, or at most two typos), the report suggests it. | | Missing headings | `[[Note#Heading]]` or `[[#Heading]]` where the heading doesn't exist. | | Broken Markdown links | Relative links to `.md` files that don't exist. `../` and `%20` are resolved. | | Ambiguous names | Two notes with the same file name. `[[name]]` can only open one of them. | | Near-duplicates | Notes whose text overlaps by about 80% or more (MinHash over 5-word shingles). | | Images without alt text | `![](…)` and `` with no `alt`. | | Empty notes | Nothing besides front matter. | | Orphans | Notes that no other note links to. `index`, `README`, `home` and `welcome` don't count as orphans. | Links inside code blocks and inline code are ignored. ## Applying the suggested fixes Command: `🩺 Vault Doctor: Apply Suggested Link Fixes`. This rewrites every broken wiki link that has a single suggestion, for example `[[Projct Plan]]` → `[[Project Plan]]`. Labels and `#heading` parts are kept. You get a list of the changes to confirm first. Notes that are open in a tab are skipped, so unsaved edits are never overwritten.

pages.title: Export and import
pages.description: Take the whole vault out as a .zip or a folder, bring in an Obsidian vault or a Notion export, and convert single files to and from many formats.
pages.md:
Your notes are plain Markdown, and they can always leave Lumen.

## The whole vault

**Export:** `⌘K → Export the whole vault…`. Pick a **.zip** download or,
where the browser can write folders (Chrome, Edge), a **folder**. Every note
and attachment is written with its folder path. A folder export goes into
a new `lumen-vault-<date>` subfolder, so nothing already in the folder you
picked is overwritten. The note you are editing is saved first.

**Import:** `⌘K → Import notes (zip / folder: Obsidian, Notion, Lumen)…`.
Pick a .zip or a folder. Lumen recognises:

| Source | Recognised by | What import does |
|---|---|---|
| Obsidian vault | an `.obsidian/` folder | notes and attachments as they are; `.obsidian/` itself is skipped |
| Notion export | most file names end in Notion's 32-character ID | IDs are removed from the names, and the links between pages are rewritten to the new names |
| Lumen export, or any folder | otherwise | everything as it is |

Everything is imported into a **new folder** (`Imported/<name>`, numbered
when that name is taken), so no existing note is ever overwritten. Two
pages that end up with the same name are numbered (`Page 2.md`).
`.git`, `.trash`, `__MACOSX` and `.DS_Store` are skipped. When the import
finishes, a message says how many notes and files came in and where.

## One document

**Out:** the *File* menu and the palette export the open note to HTML,
Word (.doc), RTF, LaTeX, reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, OPML,
slides (Reveal.js), EPUB, Jupyter (.ipynb), PowerPoint (.pptx), a static
site, and PDF (`⌘K → Print / Save as PDF…`). Right-to-left text keeps its
direction in the exported files.

**In:** open a file (`⌘O`) or drop it on the window. Besides Markdown and
text, Lumen converts HTML, RTF, CSV / TSV, JSON, XML, Word (.docx and the
older .doc), OpenDocument (.odt), PowerPoint (.pptx), Excel (.xlsx),
EPUB, PDF (with OCR for scanned pages), MHTML, OPML, LaTeX,
reStructuredText, AsciiDoc, Org-mode, Jupyter notebooks, Apple Pages /
Numbers / Keynote, Fountain screenplays and .zip archives into a Markdown
note.

## How it is tested

The vault round trip (export, then import), the Obsidian and Notion
detection, Notion's link rewrite and the duplicate-name numbering are unit
tests over `src/storage/exportAll.ts`. Each format converter has its own
tests.

pages.title: Side panels
pages.description: The file tree, outline, backlinks, tags, comments, trash and version history — what each side panel shows and how to use it.
pages.md:
Each panel has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## File tree

The left sidebar lists the notes and folders of your vault. Click a note
to open it. Each note and folder has rename and delete, and folders can
take a new note or subfolder. Select several notes to move or delete them
together; a deleted note goes to the trash, and **Undo** brings it back. In
a large vault the folders start collapsed. The sidebar's edge resizes it:
drag it, or focus it and use ← and →.

## Outline

The headings of the open note, as a tree. Click one to jump there. The
outline follows the note as you type.

## Backlinks

Every note that links to the open one with a `[[wiki-link]]`, with the
line around each link. Click a backlink to open that note.

## Tags

Every tag in the vault, from `tags:` in the frontmatter and from `#tags`
in the text, with how many notes use it. Click a tag to filter the file
tree by it.

## Comments

Comments on the shared note, when you collaborate. Each card shows the
author, the text it is anchored to and the replies. Click a card to select
that text; resolve, reply to or delete a comment from its card. Show all
comments or only the unresolved ones.

## Trash

What you deleted in the last 30 days. **Restore** puts a note back where
it was; **Delete forever** removes it now. After 30 days notes are removed
for good.

## Version history

Every kept version of the open note, newest first. A version is kept every
couple of minutes while you type, on every save and when you close the
tab. Pick a version to preview it, with how much it differs from the
current text, and **Restore this version** if you want it back.

pages.title: Workspace search (BM25 + Smart)
pages.description: Fast keyword search by default, semantic embeddings on demand.
pages.md:
`⌘K → Search workspace…` opens the workspace search dialog (the palette
shows `⇧⌘F` next to it, but that key toggles focus mode today). Three tabs:

## Search (BM25)

The default — instant keyword + filename search across every `.md` /
`.txt` in your OPFS workspace. Built on BM25+ with bigram phrase
matching, runs in a Web Worker so the UI never stalls.

- File-name match scores higher than body match.
- Highlights the matched substring inside a 160-char snippet.
- Returns the top 40 hits ordered by relevance.

## Smart (semantic)

Hybrid retrieval that fuses BM25 with cosine similarity over OpenAI
`text-embedding-3-small` vectors via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k = 60).
Finds notes that are semantically related even when the surface words
don't match — a query for *"deep learning"* surfaces a note titled
*"Neural networks"*.

To enable:

1. Switch to the **Smart** tab.
2. Click **Build index** (one-time, then incremental on subsequent runs).
3. Type your query — results re-rank in real time.

**Cost**: each chunk is embedded once and cached in IndexedDB. A 100-note
workspace embeds in ≈ 8s and ≈ 200 K tokens (≈ $0.004 with
`text-embedding-3-small`). Re-indexing only re-embeds chunks whose hash
changed.

## Ask Workspace (RAG Q&A)

Type a question, hit Enter — the dialog runs Smart search to find
relevant notes, then sends the top 8 + your question to the configured
chat model. Answers come back with `[1]` / `[2]` citations linked back
to the source notes.

**Use it for**:
- "Summarise everything I've written about onboarding."
- "Which projects mentioned that Q3 launch deadline?"
- "What did I decide about the auth provider?"

The conversation is kept in-dialog — multi-turn follow-ups remember the
prior context.
